maintopic: MEETING IN OTTAWA OF JOINT U.S.-CANADIAN COMMITTEE

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. B. Pearson (Prime Minister):
maintopic: MEETING IN OTTAWA OF JOINT U.S.-CANADIAN COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Hon. members will recall that when the President of the United States and I met in Washington last January we reviewed the work of the joint United States-Canadian committee on trade and economic affairs and agreed that it should meet again around the end of April. This committee was established in November, 1953 and normally meets alternately in Ottawa and Washington. It has now been agreed that the committee, which held its last meeting in Washington on September 20 and 21, 1963, will meet again in Ottawa on April 29 and 30.
Canada will be represented at this meeting by the Secretary of State for External Affairs and the ministers of finance, trade and commerce, industry and agriculture. The United States delegation will be led by Mr. Rusk, the secretary of state, and will consist of the secretaries of the treasury, interior, agriculture and commerce and the under secretary of state. In addition Governor Her-ter, the President's special representative for trade negotiations, and the chairman of the council of economic advisers are expected to attend as are Mr. Robertson, the chief negotiator for the Canadian government on tariffs and trade and the governor of the Bank of Canada, together with the United States ambassador in Ottawa, and our ambassador in Washington.
This meeting will provide a valuable opportunity for the ministers of both countries to review economic and trade interests of common interest and concern. Canadian ministers look forward to welcoming their United States colleagues to Ottawa and having mutually useful discussions with them.

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

maintopic: PROPOSED COMMON UNIFORM FOR ALL ARMED FORCES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I would like to address a question to the Minister of National Defence. Will the minister please advise the house whether so-called spokesmen of the Department of National Defence have been authorized by him to indicate that there shall be integration of the armed forces to the point of having a common uniform by 1967? At the same time would the minister advise me whether he has completed his inquiries into the question of leaks in regard to the white paper, which I raised some two weeks ago.

speakeroldname: Hon. Paul Hellyer (Minister of National Defence):
maintopic: PROPOSED COMMON UNIFORM FOR ALL ARMED FORCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased that the hon. gentleman has asked this question because it gives me an opportunity to correct the impression created by a newspaper story yesterday. It is true, as the press has reported, that the Department of National Defence considers July 1, 1967 as an acceptable target date for the unification of the three forces for planning purposes. I have said in the past that the integration to unification process would take approximately three to four years.
On the subject of uniforms, however, it will be some time before we start considering this matter. In the meantime there are more urgent tasks to be undertaken. A planning

Inquiries of the Ministry group is now working out the plans for the new single defence staff. Once legislation has been passed and the single defence staff is in existence, it will start to work on the formation of the headquarters organization, followed by the integration of field command organizations. So there is much work to be done before consideration can be given to the subject of uniforms.
I have no doubt, however, that the new defence staff will eventually study this matter, particularly the problem of utilizing present investments, both private and public, in uniforms and also the preservation of valued traditions. I am well aware of the great pride that service personnel, both regular and reserve, have in their uniforms, and there will be no decisions taken without full consideration of all the factors involved.

maintopic: PROPOSED COMMON UNIFORM FOR ALL ARMED FORCES
speechtext: A supplementary question, Mr. Speaker. Am I to take it from the reference to unification that the minister intends there shall be one defence force, or one armed force in this country, and there will be no distinction among the present three services or any of the units thereof?

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I made it quite clear-and this is set out in the white paper- that the integration of the defence staff is the first step toward a single unified defence force for Canada.

maintopic: PROPOSED COMMON UNIFORM FOR ALL ARMED FORCES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, would the minister please answer the second portion of my question, as to whether he has yet been able to plug the leaks in so far as the white paper and other matters are concerned.

maintopic: PROPOSED COMMON UNIFORM FOR ALL ARMED FORCES
speechtext:
This matter is quite well under control, Mr. Speaker.

maintopic: PROPOSED COMMON UNIFORM FOR ALL ARMED FORCES

I should like at this time to provide information in reply to a number of questions asked this week concerning the activities of the board of trustees in the maritime situation. These questions were raised by the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam and the hon. member for Ontario.
The first question concerns the integration of the seamen's union. The trustees have indicated that they do not favour the integration of licensed personnel in the S.I.U. To the contrary, they endorse the recommendations of Hon. Mr. Justice Norris that officers be separated from other personnel. They would favour the integration of engineers with other ships' officers if the engineers and other officers so desire. Another question raised concerned the "do not ship" list. There was no "do not ship" list in existence when the trustees were appointed, and there is not one now. Members of the trustees staff have been endeavouring to locate persons who at one time had been placed on the "do not ship" list and, where it appears they are interested, are asking them if they wish their case investigated. The trustee representatives in the hiring halls will see that the "do not ship" practice is not revived.
I have discussed with the trustees the suggestion made by the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam that they meet with the industrial relations committee of the house. The trustees have carefully considered this suggestion and feel that a meeting with this committee at this time would prejudice their efforts to achieve the objectives defined by the Maritime Transportation Unions Trustee Act. This is particularly so since much of the information in their possession is felt by the
Inquiries of the Ministry trustees to be the property of the unions they represent. The trustees naturally understand and appreciate the interest shown by members of the house in the carrying out of the difficult tasks with which they are charged.
Finally there is the question concerning hiring halls, raised by the hon. member for Ontario. The methods of hiring are governed by law,, collective agreements and the constitution of the union in question. As indicated earlier, the trustees have placed a representative in each hall who will endeavour to see that prescribed hiring arrangements are fairly followed, and the trustees will make suggestions for changes in the collective agreements and in the union constitution in this regard.
With regard to the specific question which the hon. member for Ontario posed, I understand a full member of the S.I.U. of Canada does have the privilege of accepting or refusing a particular referral. This privilege does not extend at present to probationary members. The rules governing these matters are now under review by the trustees and the unions.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to relate a certain matter to the committee and to the minister handling these estimates, especially as he is now minister responsible for this particular department. I want to refer to an exchange of correspondence, part of which is between myself and the minister's predecessor, the late Mr. Garland. It dates back to January of this year, when the Vancouver fishermen's settlement service wrote to the deputy minister of national revenue for taxation in Ottawa and pointed out certain anomalies that had arisen with respect to fishermen and the filing of income tax forms for certain years.
I think I can do no better than to read part of the text of the letter to the deputy minister in order to indicate initially what the problem was. The letter reads in part as follows:


On July 9, 1963 this office filed notices of objection with you with respect to the assessments of Andrew Karjala and Arthur Moffatt. Our objection was based on our contention that the method of averaging fishermen's tax, as set out in the Farmers' and Fishermen's Guide 1962, and on which the reassessment of the returns in question was based, was in error. To date we have had no reply to our notices of objection, although more than six months have elapsed. We now have the 1963 edition of the Farmers' and Fishermen's Guide, and also form T2011, and we note that both of these prescribe a new procedure for averaging, which leads to the same result as our original returns for Karjala and Moffatt, and which contradicts the reassessment of their returns.
We can only assume, therefore, that although the department has not seen fit to respond to our notices of objection it has nevertheless concluded that our objection was correct and has amended its own forms and instructions accordingly. We note also that the new form T2011 was printed in October, which proves that the department had accepted our interpretation at least three months ago.
I received a copy of that letter, as did the hon. member for New Westminster. I took the course of sending a copy of the letter to the late Mr. Garland in his capacity as minister of the department and asked him to deal favourably with the contention raised in the letter of January 20, 1964, from the Vancouver fishermen's settlement service. I received an interim reply that the matter was under study; then under date of February 27, 1964 I received this communication from the late Mr. Garland:
Further to my letter of 10th February, 1964, I am pleased to advise that in the case of the notices of objection filed by the Vancouver fishermen's settlement service the taxpayers will be allowed to calculate their taxes in accordance with the method set out in the 1963 edition of the Farmers' and Fishermen's Guide.
As of March 13 the Vancouver fishermen's settlement service had not received any communication from the minister to the effect that he agreed with their contention. I do not know the reason for the failure to answer, but I note that the same thing occurred before with respect to the original notices of objection, in that no reply was received.
In fact what has happened is that undoubtedly these two fishermen, Karjala and Moffatt, were not the only fishermen who filed income tax forms for the year 1962 as prescribed in the Farmers' and Fishermen's Guide. Undoubtedly many thousands of farmers in Canada as well as many hundreds of fishermen filed income tax declarations according to the 1962 guide, and undoubtedly many of them had their returns reassessed.
It seems to me that there may well be thousands of people in Canada who are not aware of the exact situation because the minister or the department have not communicated the specific information in any public way. Certainly they have not done so

to the Vancouver fishermen's settlement service, which raised the matter in the first place. Therefore I would think there must be thousands of people in Canada who, on the basis of the erroneous method of calculation in the Farmers' and Fishermen's Guide for 1962, have paid countless dollars in taxes which they should not have paid because their returns were reassessed by the department.
I am sure if the farmers and fishermen of this country knew that the department or the minister had come to the conclusion that the reassessments made on the basis of the 1962 Farmers' and Fishermen's Guide were in fact in error they would like to have the opportunity to re-examine their position and to re-file in accordance with the revised interpretation contained in the 1963 edition, which was authorized as correct by the late minister, Mr. Garland, in February of this year in the letter he sent to me.
I only raise this matter in a public way to point out the situation and to ask the minister to see that the original notices of objection or letters from the Vancouver fishermen's settlement service are replied to; and perhaps to make a public declaration of what the fact is so that those farmers and fishermen who may have paid countless thousands of dollars in taxes which they should not have paid will have the opportunity to reassess their position and re-file their forms for that year. There has apparently been an error on the part of the Department of National Revenue, and the farmers and fishermen should have the opportunity to get back a few dollars for their own pockets.

I have two questions for the minister, one related to the item we have just passed and one related specifically to this item. One of the problems of the revenue department, which we all understand, is this question of making tax levies equitable. The dividing line is sometimes not

Supply-National Revenue easy to determine. There are two industries in Canada that I believe are suffering from inequitable decisions by the taxation department.
The first is the soft drinks industry. I found it rather difficult to speak to the late minister on this subject because he was so honest in his own approach to it he found it difficult to take a position other than that which had been common practice, because his own business background related to this industry. We have across this country a number of small industries producing soft drinks. Their product is subject to sales tax. Their chief competition comes from soft drinks that are made in the home, the constituents of which are purchased in food stores. I am thinking of Kool Ade and a number of other products of that type which are not subject to tax.
The increased cost of sugar and the increased cost of operations have put many of these small soft drink companies in a financial position where they are likely to go out of business. There is a limit to which they can raise the price of the product and they find it impossible to carry on in a profitable way because they have to pay sales tax on their product, which is in direct competition with a product which is not subject to tax.
This brings me to the second point which I should like to bring to the attention of the minister. It relates to fresh fruit juices that are imported in concentrated form in bulk packages and then reconstituted and sold mostly through our dairies. In examining this question we find that the canned concentrated fruit juice sold in food stores is not subject to tax, and neither is the powdered concentrate. Of course, fresh fruits are not subject to tax. However, when this same concentrated fruit juice comes into the country in bulk containers and is reconstituted it is subject to excise tax. This seems to be an inequitable situation.
It has been brought to my attention that some United States firms have completed large contracts with some of our large food distributing stores, particularly of the supermarket type, under which these stores are importing tax free reconstituted juice from the United States in 32-ounce containers. When our Canadian dairies import the same constituted juice that these United States companies are using and reconstitute it themselves, it is subject to tax. I think this is something about which we ought to be very careful because unnecessarily it results in a tremendous drain on United States dollars. If we imported the concentrated juice and packaged it here using our own labour, we would not only save foreign exchange but we would

also give work to a number of our people. I mention this because I believe the government should look at the matter closely.
I hope the government will try to make the situation more equitable so far as the soft drink industry is concerned and will also give consideration to the question of these imported concentrated fruit juices. I am sure any action would be not only helpful to those who are interested in seeing that a greater amount of fruit is included in our diets, but it would also be more equitable treatment to an important part of the business community of this country.

I think the house owes a debt of gratitude to the hon. member for Northwest Territories who, knowing the conditions of the Eskimo to a degree that no other white man has ever known finds himself a representative of theirs in parliament, to the

Supply-Northern Affairs hon. member for Yukon with his wide knowledge, as well as the hon. members for Pontiac-Temiscamingue and Peace River. The representations of these hon. members deserve the serious consideration of the minister and of parliament. Indeed, this is a matter so serious in its import that the Prime Minister himself should make clear the views of the government.
I am not entering into any difficulties as between the federal government and the provincial government of Quebec but I am joining with the hon. gentlemen who have spoken to express the strongest condemnation of the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources, which in what it has done even to date shows a disregard for an aboriginal people that cannot be justified. Eskimos are not serfs; they are not political captives or pawns to be shoved about at the will or the whim of a government or governments. They are Canadians.
I read the other day with a great deal of interest the views expressed by the minister in an address at St. Catharines. That address was filled with the wisdom that comes from years of experience in public life. The heading is, "Laing says Canada is envy of world". The minister said in this speech:
Canada is the envy of the world, a country everyone outside its boundaries thinks is a superb place and whose future only those inside our boundaries doubt.
He was speaking to the south Ontario Liberal association. Then he made some observations, when he got away from national issues, and said this:
Our entire safety lies in a government of laws, and not men.
Never were truer words spoken by him. I am going to ask him to carry out the terms of the great principles that he enunciated. I will read what he said again:
Our entire safety lies in a government of laws, and not men.
What have we here? Have we a government, in so far as the Eskimos are concerned, of laws, not men? Can these people, who are within the sole jurisdiction of the federal parliament, be transferred, bartered away, whatever the terms, to another legislative body? Where is the constitution of this country, if this can be done? Are they to be mandatorily, and without regard to their feelings, transported into another jurisdiction? What would happen if any group of Canadians that was exclusively under the jurisdiction of a province was transferred to another jurisdiction? Can it be done?
Well, Mr. Chairman, I have before me the only recent case dealing with the subject of the transfer of jurisdiction, administrative or

otherwise. I shall refer to it after first referring to the case to which various hon. members have alluded. That is the case decided in 1939; it was a reference as to whether the term "Indians" in head 24 of section 91 of the British North America Act-

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, would the right hon. Leader of the Opposition mind giving me the reference to the case again?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
I am just coming to that. It was a reference as to whether the term "Indians" in head 24 of section 91 of the British North America Act, which gives exclusive jurisdiction to the federal government, includes Eskimo inhabitants of the province of Quebec. It is to be found in the Canada Supreme Court Reports, 1939, at page 104 and following. This is a very interesting situation. In 1939 the province of Quebec contended that it was not right or legal or constitutional for the government of Canada to give the government of Quebec the responsibility to look after the Eskimos in that province. They claimed that this responsibility could not be placed on their shoulders. The government of Canada argued that an Eskimo was not an Indian and that therefore the exclusive jurisdiction over Indians did not apply to Eskimos.
I am not going to read from the case, except to point out that it is a most interesting one. One goes back as far as 1763, and on the 8th day of June of that year a discussion took place concerning the trade carried on by the French on the coast of Labrador. With regard to that discussion it is reported that they carried on "an extensive trade with the Eskimo Indians in oil, furs, etc. (in which they allowed Your Majesty's subjects no share)". Then later on Sir Hugh Palliser referred to the Eskimos as Indians. On April 10, 1772, Governor Shuldham referred to them as the Eskimo Indians. And so on throughout the years.
The Hudson's Bay Company made a full investigation regarding the peoples under their jurisdiction and came to the conclusion that the proper description of the Eskimo was within the classification of "Indian". Finally in 1879 correspondence passed between Sir John A. Macdonald and Sir Hector Langevin on the subject of the Eskimo on the north shore of the St. Lawrence, and throughout the correspondence "Eskimo Indians" is employed as a description, as it had been employed for 100 years in official and other documents.
The interesting situation was this. The province of Quebec said, "The Eskimos belong to you". The government of Canada of that day said, "No, the Eskimos do not belong to us and we are not responsible for them". They fought the case, and the Supreme Court of Canada held that Eskimos came within the

descriptive word "Indians". So the government, the parliament of Canada, has exclusive jurisdiction; and in these days of constitutional discussion the government of Canada is the first in this regard to brush aside the constitution, to deny their exclusive jurisdiction and, under the guise of pretending that what they are doing is entering into an agreement, they would turn over the administration to a jurisdiction that has no right to exercise any power over these people, beyond the usual powers that a province has over subjects or people within its boundaries.
In order to do this the minister says, "We can enter into an agreement with the province". I am most anxious to hear the opinion of the law officers of the crown in this connection. I say that no reading of the judgment in the case of the attorney general of Nova Scotia and the attorney general of Canada reported in 1951 Canada Supreme Court Reports, page 31, can lead one to believe that the parliament of Canada or the government of Canada can by a simple agreement get rid of, transfer, assign or sublet any of its exclusive jurisdiction. While I do not usually read the headnote alone, I am going to do so on this occasion, Mr. Chairman. Every lawyer knows that it is always most important to read all the case rather than just the headnote, but the headnote does epitomize the decision of the Supreme Court of Canada. It reads:
The parliament of Canada and each provincial legislature is a sovereign body within its sphere, possessed of exclusive jurisdiction to legislate with regard to the subject matters assigned to it under section 91 or section 92, as the case may be.
This is the important thing. The province of Nova Scotia thought it could transfer some jurisdiction to the federal parliament:
Neither is capable therefore of delegating to the other the powers with which it has been vested nor of receiving from the other the powers with which the other has been vested.
There is just no question about this. All the evasive uncertainty that has been displayed in this matter does not take cognizance of the fact that the parliament of Canada or the government of Canada cannot deal with fellow Canadians in a cavalier, unjust manner without regard to their views. There has been a suggestion here that a referendum might take place on the basis of the 1951 case. No matter what the referendum might declare, this act could not be justified, under the authority to which I have referred. I cannot understand this. These are aboriginal people in a country which has undertaken not only the responsibilities inherent in the bill of rights but is a member of the United Nations, and Canada intends by this action to breach the greatest principle of all.
Supply-Northern Affairs
I have listened to the argument in this connection, and the more I look at the minister of northern affairs the more I am convinced that he is convinced he has a most unsalutary job on his hands, that of trying to explain why this action is justified. As a matter of fact, in light of principles such as he enunciated in that speech, embodying as they do his views throughout his life as I have known it for many years, in his own heart he cannot justify this. I raise it to a level higher than an emotional one; I raise it to the constitutional level. The government cannot do this; they dare not do this. They cannot take people like this and shove them around as pawns in order to meet the needs of the moment.
I go further than that. Even if they agreed to this it would not be within the constitutional limitations defined bv the 1951 case. It would be a case of self-determination. I have heard the Secretary of State for External Affairs speaking of self-determination somewhere else in the world. What about trying it in Canada? In this case, even though the government determine upon this course the constitution will not allow it, if I read the case in 1951 aright, and there has been no challenge that I am reading it wrongly.
Now, Mr. Chairman, why is this the case? I presume it is because the government felt these people would be voiceless serfs. In other words, they would have no one to speak for them. But they have in the person of the hon. member for Northwest Territories and other members. The minister has not denied something he was asked the other day. He was asked whether or not, when he saw the Eskimos, he did not find them opposed to this action. He did not deny that, and the interpretation of his failure to deny it becomes very clear.
I am not resting the case of these people on the basis of any arguments as between the government of Canada and the desires of any province. I am resting it on the constitutional right of these people to have their rights respected by parliament. How are we going to justify this? Today we hear more and more, and in stronger terms than ever before, that the constitution must be maintained. Yet at the very time this is going on these poor people on the shores of the Arctic are being told that the constitution belongs to others but not to them. That is in effect what they are being told, and the government cannot justify this. Strong arguments on the law have been made by the hon. member for Pontiac-Temiscamingue. He pointed out the circumstances and he pointed out the law.

Supply-Northern Affairs
We cannot get any information. I am going to ask, Mr. Chairman, a few questions and we will want answers to these questions before this item dealing with these poor untutored fellow Canadians passes. Are negotiations now going on between the federal government and the government of Quebec in connection with the financial arrangements? Has the federal government offered to pay 50 per cent of the cost of the administration? Does the government of Quebec ask for 100 per cent of those costs? Do the prospective arrangements call for transferral of federal property, including hospitals, schools and administrative buildings, and on what terms? These are questions to which we have the right to answers. The government are talking of the constitution as though it belonged to us, the white race. This is a constitution which belongs to all Canadians without regard to race. I make this appeal to the government: Do not think that because they are few in number their votes do not count. Do not treat them as chattels to be pushed around, their constitutional rights denied.
That is the appeal we make, far and above the things that separate as between the federal government and any of the provinces. That is what is at stake here in trying to get information from the government. They say that parliament is being held up. Last evening the Prime Minister spoke of obstruction. I could read some of his statements on the subject of obstruction through the years when he was in opposition. It is not obstruction to stand for the rights of the people in the House of Commons. We are not going to be placed in the position of having the government, hiding behind a smokescreen of obstruction, at the same time, while hiding behind it surreptitiously and clandestinely take away the rights of these people. We are not going to have that. We are going to have this matter cleared up and the Minister of Justice is the one who can do it.
I am going to refer to an article in L'Action by Mr. Poliquin on February 21 last. He referred to the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources and the minister of natural resources for Quebec having a five hour meeting the day before. On the question of consultation Mr. Poliquin, who was present, reports Mr. Levesque as having said:
It our Eskimos are advised previously of any decision and given detailed explanation, we are in accord.
That is the attitude of the minister of natural resources, Mr. Levesque.
But if you consider their lack of information, their complete dependence on federal civil servants, and if consulting them seems a sort of referendum, then this should not be done, for it would be inapplicable and artificial.


No matter whether there was such consultation it would still remain a travesty on the constitution. Mr. Levesque went on to say:
On the other hand, we are quite sure that in accepting the principle of the transfer the federal authorities have no intention of ruining it by such procedures.
That means that those on the government benches have agreed to this and they must place the facts before us no longer wrapped in an enigma of uncertainty. We want to know what the facts are. We want to know whether these aboriginal people are to be treated as persons, as people-

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: As Canadians.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
-or are they simply to be in the position of inanimate things, of chattels, who are to have their course determined by the will of the master? That is the issue here, the constitution of Canada; and the constitution must be upheld. It is not to be deviated from, it is not to be circumvented by the political exigencies of the moment. What did the Minister of Justice say on this occasion? Mr. Poliquin goes on to say in his report:
One can hardly call it a love scene. In this atmosphere the... conference opened in the west block. They took turns provoking each other. About 6.30 p.m. Levesque had had enough. He prepared to leave. He was fed up with the stubbornness of Mr. Laing.
Then the Minister of Justice came into the picture.
Mr. Guy Favreau at this point intervened with: "We agree judicially, administratively and financially. Why burn the bridge between us?"

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Oh, oh.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
That is what Mr. Poliquin reported and he was there. I was not. The two ministers were. They will be able to give their revised version of this event. Then the article goes on to say:
Discussion went on for 90 minutes. Nothing was decided.
Then it says that Mr. Levesque was "bombarded" by the press. That is a good expression. Mr. Levesque is reported as having said:
I abhor a pseudo-democratic consultation, which would give the Eskimos the right of veto on this transfer, and which would be a farce.
I say, and I am not in full agreement with my colleagues in this regard, that I do not think consultation in any way meets the situation, but certainly consultation would have been at least a step forward. But they are not to receive that. They are to be told: You are Eskimos; you have no rights under the constitution.
Sir, we are going to find out about this. I am not entering into a discussion as to the matters that may be in issue between the

federal and provincial government. I am putting this to the Minister of Justice directly. I do not know whether he was one of distinguished counsel on that case in 1951. No, he was not on that one, but he was one of the law officers and I am asking him to interpret that case. I know I must not ask the Minister of Justice to give his opinion of the law, but it would be interesting, though, if he should try to say that that case does not deny the very thing that is being done here.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: He has made a facial expression but you cannot tell whether it is yes or no.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
If the Minister of Justice will not give an opinion then I ask any of the legal members of the house to read the case. It does not require much interpretation to understand these words, and I repeat them:
The parliament of Canada and each provincial legislature Is a sovereign body.. .Neither is capable therefore of delegating to the other the powers-
And so on. Of course, in order to explain this away they will say that they are not delegating power over the Eskimos; they are just delegating the right to exercise the power of administration over them. What else is left? No more important matter will come before this parliament than the welfare of 2,500 Eskimos. How can the government deal with them in this way and then go to the United Nations and say that Canada stands against discrimination? To treat these people in this way is the crassest demonstration of discrimination in that it denies that the constitution of Canada, which is my birthright and the birthright of all Canadians, applies to Eskimos. That is my argument.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
As a relative newcomer to this house I have heard some moving and dramatic speeches. Seldom, however, have I heard a more moving and dramatic one than the one made by the Leader of the Opposition. He has gone through the history of this issue and put the constitutional position in very clear terms. He has said that the constitutional position and the decisions of the highest authorities must be respected. He has given us a very dramatic and moving demonstration of the need to respect human rights, pointing out that the Eskimos involved in the administration of northern affairs are not mere pawns.
In the short time I have been in this house, Mr. Chairman, I have observed a few things. I observe that today the hon. member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm is not here when his leader speaks in this house on this matter. I have heard the hon. member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm persistently accuse this government and press this government as to why it was not going to proceed with this measure, which the leader of his party has said would be such a wrong thing to do. The Conservative party in this house speaks with two voices. If parliament comes into disrespect it is because of a lack of sincerity. I have seldom witnessed

Supply-Northern Affairs a greater exercise in sanctimonious hypocrisy than that put on by the Leader of the Opposition.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
I have sat here often and heard the encouragement of the questioning by the hon. member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Mont-calm in an effort to embarrass this government when it was taking a very carefully considered position on this matter. I am proud of the position the minister of northern affairs has taken. It is fortunate that he is most reasonable. He is also, Mr. Chairman, as cognizant of human rights as any hon. member of this house.
Surely it ill-behooves the opposition in this house to speak, as I have heard them on other matters, with two voices. One voice attacks the government because it does not follow an aggressive ultranationalist policy which would do a great deal of harm to this country. The other voice is the more sensible voice of conscience, which says there are human rights, that there is a constitutional position. I am glad to hear the constitutional position so well put forward. This kind of thing, in my opinion, does not do credit to this house when two voices come forward on a matter as important as this. The position of the government, a position which I am able to support, is one of careful consideration of all aspects of the problem and full consideration of provincial and federal rights. Certainly, to my knowledge, no action has been taken which is inconsistent with that.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Bring on another seal.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, this is a very delicate matter which everybody should discuss with the utmost coolness and moderation since human beings are involved.
Thus, I am not blaming the hon. member who has spoken before me for having become a bit irritated because in certain quarters, an attempt was made to make political capital of negotiations between Quebec and Ottawa with respect to the Eskimos.
When I first came to this house, directly from the bar, I never would have believed that this matter would be examined without at least finding out all the facts, the policy of the government and its position from a legal point of view.
I say that the hon. member for Yukon (Mr. Nielsen), who is perhaps the one who most bitterly criticized the attitude of the government in the house, has always intimated something which is false both in fact and in law. He was scandalized and he took for granted that the government intends to proceed with a jurisdictional transfer of Eskimo affairs. On the basis of this false premise, he accused the government of not being concerned about the rights of the Eskimos and of just simply signing an agreement to rid government of its jurisdiction.
I say that such statements are a hateful betrayal of the truth, of the facts and of the law.
It is true, Mr. Chairman, that under section 91 of the B.N.A. Act, the legislative jurisdiction concerning the Indians rests with the federal government. It is also true that in 1939, where the matter was referred to the supreme court, neither the Quebec government nor the Ottawa government wanted to look after the Eskimos. It is also true that the supreme court, at that time, stated that for the purpose of section 91 the Eskimo people were Indians. Therefore, the related jurisdiction, in the legislative view point in particular, rested with the federal government, and more precisely with the parliament of Canada.
What is not true is, first of all, that the present government tried or is trying to make a transfer of jurisdiction. Neither is it true that we are trying to lay down conditions for the administration of Eskimo affairs in the far north and that the government would forget or rather would bypass those human beings, those Canadians, because the Eskimos are Canadians.
There was no treason, no attempt to get rid of that jurisdiction. The Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker) referred to a decision of the supreme court to the effect that delegation of powers between federal

and provincial authorities-delegation or exchange of powers, as defined or described in sections 91 and 92 of the British North America Act-was illegal.
It is true that it was stated, in that case, that the two governments are sovereign in their respective fields and that, under the constitution, a provincial government cannot delegate its powers to the federal government in a field that is subject to legislative jurisdiction under section 92, just like the federal government cannot delegate its powers to the provincial government in a field which comes under its own jurisdiction according to section 91.
Therefore, this prohibits such agreements, such contracts, under which constitutional powers would be exchanged without being authorized by an amendment of the Canadian constitution.
But what happens in the same case? It has been decided that nothing prevents the federal government, in the exercise of its own jurisdiction, from selecting a body of the provincial government as its representative, its agent to exercise, in accordance with conditions laid down by the federal government, a federal jurisdiction; and the fact that this agent acts on behalf of the federal government is not unlawful, but on the contrary it is completely in accordance with the constitution.
Conversely, it is clear that the provincial government which is entrusted with the administration of certain civic rights may delegate, when necessary, to the federal government or to an agent or a department of the federal government, the power to act as its representative for the purposes of exercising its jurisdiction. It is simply a delegation of powers and a mandate is merely being conferred, on behalf of the provincial government, to the main agent. It is quite clear and simple and there is nothing more to it.
What, then, is the matter involved here? It is merely for the moment a draft agreement under which the Quebec government would agree to look after the administration of Eskimo affairs in the far north, on behalf of the federal government.
The federal government maintains its jurisdiction to such an extent, gives up so little of its authority and is so anxious to carry out its responsibilities, of which it is aware, that this administration by the Quebec government will only be conducted, as specified moreover, in the draft agreement, under conditions laid down by the federal government. Therefore, it is in the exercise of its jurisdiction and in order to discharge responsibilities towards the Eskimos that the federal government imposes conditions on the province of Quebec in that administration,
Supply-Northern Affairs and the federal government will be satisfied only when the provincial government accepts them.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, may I ask a question?
Has the government of the province of Quebec accepted to have conditions thus imposed by the federal government?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
That is my understanding under the preliminary agreement which has already been mentioned by the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources (Mr. Laing), myself or our government as well as by the representatives of Quebec.
One only has to read the statement made in this house by the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources to understand. It laid down the policy to be followed. We will be satisfied only when there has been sufficient consultation with the Eskimos and only at that moment, any agreement will simply be within a definite framework established by the federal government, and the province will take over administration of a sector, that of the Eskimo affairs, in cases limited to northern Quebec.
That is nothing new. That policy is already accepted by this government and was applied in the past in a very useful and efficient way by the government which preceded us under the direction of the leader of today's official opposition.
I have in mind, for instance, an agreement concerning Indians under which the federal government transferred to some provinces the field of education of Indian children-

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: No application at all. [Translation]

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: -or when the Indian community development was entrusted to provincial governments. Those are useful agreements, but they are agreements under which the provincial governments involved purely and simply become mandatories of the federal government to administer a sector or a part of Indian affairs. They do not do this on their own authority, but rather under the authority of the federal government.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
With respect, would the minister permit a question which is very pertinent to this point. Is it not a fact that any agreements that are in effect between the federal government and the provincial governments are only because of legislation, section 113 of the Indian Act, by which parliament gave to the government the right to negotiate agreements in accordance with the Indian Act? The point I make is that the

Supply-Northern Affairs federal government negotiated those agreements only because parliament authorized it to do so.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Such agreements are made within the administrative authority of the federal government and that was dealt with by the supreme court in 1939, when both governments were refusing to look after the Eskimos-

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: On a point of order, Mr. Chairman, something obviously happened in the translation booth and we did not get the English translation of the words following the question put by the hon. member for Peace River. Would the minister mind going over them again?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
I listen so infrequently to my own words-I hope that will not be considered as a defect or a fault-that I do not always remember the exact words, but only the ideas I try to convey.

Mr. Chairman, I was saying that the agreements which were and continue to be made in regard to Indian affairs are made in the framework of the exercise, by the federal government, of its administrative jurisdiction in the field of Indian affairs.
But to dispel the concern my learned friend showed a while ago, I would add this: If at present the federal government administers Eskimo affairs, it is because the supreme court, by a decision rendered in 1939, allocated this responsibility to the federal government.
And in the same way that no one can question our right to deal with Eskimo affairs through agents, representatives, intermediaries-because of course it is not the government who must go in northern Canada to look after Eskimo affairs, it may be civil servants, agents or representatives-I do not see why, as long as the decision quoted by the Leader of the Opposition is not against that and that there is no transfer of jurisdiction, we could not use, in the same way, a provincial government to manage Eskimo affairs, within the limits of specific territories, and this according to the standards and-I repeat-conditions that will be prescribed by the federal government.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, may I direct a question to the minister? Since the administrative fields which are to be transferred deal with education, health services, and so on, am I to understand that the minister, when he says that those fields-and I refer especially

to education-will be managed by the provincial government, but on the terms prescribed by the federal government? In other words, will the federal government, in the education field, dictate to the provincial government how to discharge its responsibilities?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, as regards education, my learned friend may be assured that the fundamental rights of the Eskimos will be respected. That is, indeed, the first condition we laid down.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Answer the question.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, some apprehension was voiced with regard to the religious angle. Now, that has always been the first care, not only of those who represented the federal government, but also of the representatives of Quebec, who agree that the respective faiths of all Eskimos concerned would be respected and that there would be no infringement of their freedom of religion.
Besides, those who know Quebec are aware that in this province educational and religious matters are essentially linked, and there is no question about it, to our mind, because we would not have it any other way.
As to the children's education, the Eskimo parents' wishes will be regarded, and the same principle will apply in respect of their faith. In short, they will be treated in the same way as the Indian parents and children.
And if hon. members still have any doubt or worry concerning the contents of any possible agreement, which would only be signed after consulting the Eskimos, it will be my learned and hon. friend the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources, who will deal with it.
Should there be any apprehension with regard to the substance of a possible agreement I am authorized to say that it is the wish of the government to give the house the assurance that the text of any such agreement concerning Eskimo administration in the far north of Quebec will not be implemented until it has been tabled in the house, and time and opportunity has been afforded to any hon. member to test the confidence of the house in the government, if any hon. member wishes to do so.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
There are two or three points I should like to make in connection with the minister's declaration. But first I should like to refer to the intervention made by the hon. member for Carleton who felt he should introduce some colour into the debate this afternoon by drawing attention in some fashion or other to the absence from the chamber of the hon. member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm. I should like to say

to the hon. member tor Carleton that my hon. friend told me yesterday he had a speaking engagement outside this city today. In accordance with that engagement he left this building much earlier this afternoon. Therefore any conclusion the hon. member may have wished to make, whether of a colourful nature or not, is at once odious and entirely untrue. My hon. friend is as legitimately absent this afternoon as the hon. member for Carleton often is. So let there be an end to that canard.
As to what was said by the minister, we should appreciate clarification of certain points. When the hon. gentleman indicated that the conditions of the administration would be imposed by the federal government -that the provincial government would merely be the agent of the federal government-did he mean the preliminary agreement envisaged that there would be no discretion on the part of the agent as to determination of policy? Is this a general mandate? Who is to furnish the funds, and will there be an accounting of the funds used in the discharge of this administration? Who will determine the norms for education? Will the Eskimo children in this part of Canada receive the same level of facilities, technical or otherwise, as are being provided for instance at Inuvik, or will there be one policy for Eskimo children in the northern part of Quebec and another policy for those who live elsewhere? We want to be given answers to these questions.
The minister, in his eloquence, was skilful in sliding around the questions put to him by my hon. friend from Pontiac-Temisca-mingue. He said the rights of the Eskimos will be respected and that the desires of the Eskimo parents will be respected. But he said nothing about the policy and the administrative conditions to be followed and imposed by the federal government. These are questions which demand an answer.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
I had proposed to deal today mainly with the matter of the constitutional position of the government in relation to the entente or agreement contemplated. The hon. member may be sure that his questions will be answered and dealt with by my colleague the minister of northern affairs whose estimates we are now discussing-I should have said "supplementary estimates" but such is the length of the discussion that I always think we are really discussing the main estimates. Those questions which the hon. member raised will be dealt with by the minister responsible for the particular department concerned.
Supply-Northern Affairs [Translation]

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I do not believe the minister can resort to such excuses, since he tried to justify the government's position and he indicated the federal government had an absolute right to send an agent or an administrative officer. It is precisely on this point I am asking what will be the rights and powers of this agent, for an agent cannot have more powers than the principal.
This is why I am asking whether this agreement, or this preliminary agreement, provides administrative or political independence for the agent. Otherwise, there will be no principal and agent basis, but an agreement whereby the federal government will delegate the entire administration to the province. This is why I insist on these particulars; if not, the principle advocated by the minister, who, in his argument, holds-I do not mean that he is trying to deceive the house-that he could elude the judgment quoted by the Leader of the Opposition will go by the board.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I wish to say a word or two with respect to what the minister has said and particularly in regard to what he has not said. We have had no explanation from him as yet, nor have we had it from the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources, with respect to what the government's intentions are in regard to the Eskimos of new Quebec. We still have not received any answers and the arguments that were presented by the right hon. Leader of the Opposition have not been answered. The minister has thrown up a smokescreen in an endeavour to say that because Indian people have been treated in a certain respect with regard to educational matters and health and welfare, Eskimo people can be treated the same way. The minister nods his head in the affirmative, but I am sure he must realize that the Eskimo people cannot be treated, constitutionally, in the same fashion as the Indian people, because there is a specific exclusion with regard to these people in the Indian Act. If he will read section 113-and I am sure he must have done so when he was minister of citizenship and immigration-he will see that specific exclusion. My colleague from Peace River points out that section 4 also has applicability.
The minister is saying that because the government has been in the habit of dealing with educational, jurisdictional transfers with regard to Indian people, he can do the same thing with regard to Eskimo people. This is false and wrong. While section 113 of the Indian Act, an act passed by this parliament, authorizes this specifically, it specifically excludes Eskimo people. I will read, for the

Supply-Northern Affairs benefit of the minister and the committee, section 4 of the Indian Act, which sets forth the following:
This act does not apply to the race of aborigines commonly referred to as Eskimos.
How, therefore, can the minister justify his so-called argument in reply to the constitutional points made by the Leader of the Opposition and by the hon. member for Peace River by saying, "Because we have done it with the Indian people, we can do it now with the Eskimos"? Quite the contrary is the case. The parliament of Canada has authorized jurisdiction with regard to educational matters to be delegated to the provinces, if you will, but it has specifically excluded that power with respect to Eskimos. So there is still a good deal to be answered by the minister. The minister, as the person responsible for safeguarding the constitutional rights of these people, is called upon to answer specifically why he considers the government is justified in transferring any jurisdiction whatsoever in regard to the Eskimo people, wherever they are situated in Canada, whether it is the province of Quebec, the province of Manitoba, or indeed in any other location in Canada.
I can tell the minister this, which the hon. member for Northwest Territories has already told him and members of this house on a previous occasion. The Eskimo people do not regard as their home any particular province, neither the province of Quebec, nor Manitoba nor Newfoundland. They regard as their home the north. The Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources, while he was asked the question on occasion after occasion, has yet not risen to confirm the assurances that he gave to those people in Fort Chimo when he visited them, namely the assurance to the Eskimos in that region who did not want any transfer of jurisdiction-

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, would the hon. member permit a question? Where is the word "assurance" involved in the statement I made? What assurance did I make when I visited them?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
Let me read it to the minister; his memory has obviously failed him for a moment. I have in my hand Hansard for December 16 last year, when he said, as reported on page 5976, when making a statement on his estimates:
I found that the Eskimos made the following demands upon me, that no change from the federal administration to provincial control be made without further consulting them. I found that their opinions were so definite that I told them we would not make a change without discussing the situation further with them...They did not want a change made.


I took it from that and from the quotations which have been made of the minister's remarks in the press across this country, that this amounted to an assurance to those people that no change would be made unless they were consulted at every stage as to the government's intentions. They have been bandying this word "consultation" about and we are now in a complete maze, because what the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources means by "consultation" is quite obviously different from what the Minister of Justice means by "consultation", which again is different from what the Prime Minister means by that word; and it certainly is widely different from the views obviously held by the minister of resources for Quebec, Mr. Levesque. He said, as late as yesterday, as reported in the Winnipeg Tribune that jurisdiction over the Eskimos in Quebec had gone to the federal government in 1939 by a court decision, because there was an international scandal over mistreatment of Canadian Eskimos, and Quebec at the time was not interested in doing anything about it. In the same article the press quotes him as giving a flat refusal to the request for a referendum on the takeover, and he also said there had been a rampant campaign by people tied to the federal government against this little provincial government which is supposed to be coming in to deprive the Eskimos of everything else. Then further he said that they would never accept a referendum to help a bunch of hypocrites to get the answer they want, but that he will go into consultation about anything else.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Would the hon. member permit a question. Was the hon. member in the house when the minister of northern affairs reported on the terms of the free understanding between Quebec and Ottawa, in which he recited the definition of consultation, that there could be no other definition than this one?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
I certainly was in the house on that day. If the date has escaped the minister it was March 4, and I was shocked to read what the minister had placed on the record. I am sure that is not what the minister wants, nor is it what his departmental officials want. Because what he read into the record on that day was this, that the extent of the consultation will be that the terms and provisions of a fait accompli, of an agreement which had been executed between the two governments would be explained-explained, mind you- to the Eskimo people. That is what the minister said, and if that is consultation, I fail to appreciate how the rights of these people are

being protected. I fail to see how that statement of March 4 can be reconciled with what the minister said on December 16.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: For the purpose of the record, will the hon. member agree that when he stated a few minutes ago what the minister of northern affairs is alleged by him to have said, he was not reading from any text but was quoting extemporaneously?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
I have Hansard for March 4 in front of me, and for the purpose of accuracy I would point out the minister said this, as reported on page 506:
The consultation, that is the communication of the terms of the agreement, excluding however the financial provisions thereof, and the receiving of the views and comments of the Eskimos concerned, will be made through a commission, consisting of one or more members appointed jointly by the federal and provincial governments. The functions of this commission will be to explain the conditions of the agreement, as well as the programs for the future, in terms clear to the Eskimos and to interpret and report to the two governments on the views and comments which will have been expressed to the commission.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Is that not consultation?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: If that is the extent of the consultation, then I am afraid this government is sadly lacking-

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Read on.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
Well, there is no point in my reading the whole thing because the minister himself put it on the record. However, I will read the last paragraph of the minister's statement, which will not take up too much time of the committee.
Both governments agree that such consultation is a prior condition to the execution of the agreement. After the commission has reported, the two governments must also agree upon what modifications and recommendations suggested in the report should be accepted and included in the final text of the instrument of transfer.
When the minister put this statement on the record on March 4 he said no agreement had been reached. There was not even an agreement to agree; it was a consensus. Now we find the Minister of Justice referring today to a draft agreement, a draft agreement that I suggest-he can correct me if I am wrong

has already been prepared in the absence of the constitution of the commission to which the minister referred on March 4. So that there already exists a draft agreement-

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
On a question of privilege, I never referred to a draft agreement. What I said, and I have my words as translated from the French, was that the government wished to give an assurance that any agreement which may be made with the government of Quebec for the administration of the Eskimos will not be implemented until it has been
Supply-Northern Affairs tabled in the house, and time and opportunity has been afforded to any hon. member to test the confidence of the house and the government, if any member should be disposed to do so. That is what I said.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: The Minister of Justice cannot wriggle out of the words he used before he started reading from the text because as Hansard will show, he definitely referred to a draft agreement before he started reading from any text. If I am not correct, let the Minister of Justice now stand in his place and tell the members of this committee that there is in existence no draft agreement between the two governments. I challenge him to do that.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I think the Minister of Justice has no reason to have any such knowledge of this matter at all; but I do, and I categorically deny that there is any draft agreement whatsoever existing at the present time.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
This is fine, Mr. Chairman. We have been attempting for weeks and weeks and weeks to get answers similar to that which the minister has just given, and now we are getting them. If anyone wonders why we take time on these supplementary estimates surely the actions of the government are full explanation. The Minister of Justice would not rise in his place and give us that assurance, but the minister of northern affairs had the courage to do so.
I presume the Minister of Justice intends to follow the procedure set forth by the minister of northern affairs so far as the so-called consultation with the Eskimos is concerned. He is so generous as to assure the members of this committee that the government will show us the agreement. He will table it in the house so that we can have a look at it-not so that we can exercise our constitutional right as the parliament of Canada to ratify any such agreement; not so that we can-

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Again on a question of privilege, Mr. Chairman, what was said was that the agreement, if and when it is made, will not be implemented before any member of this house could test the confidence of the government as to its terms and implementation.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
Again, Mr. Chairman, try as
the minister might he cannot evade the words already in Hansard and which I copied down myself. He said that the text of the agreement would be, and here I quote him, "tabled to check the confidence of the house in the government".

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
To test it.

Supply-Northern Affairs

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
This will be after the agreement has been executed, after the Eskimo people have been bypassed, after parliament has been bypassed and after the constitution of this country has been completely disregarded by the government. This, sir, is the intention of the government.
The minister speaks of critical remarks which are hateful. I suggest to the members of this committee that it is hateful to see the evasion of the truth to which this house has been submitted by members occupying the treasury benches, not only on this question but on others. Questions are asked and not answered at all. If they are answered they are distorted, just as this one has been.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: That is what you are doing now.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: I suggest to the minister that he has been guilty of distorting the facts of this case, otherwise the dozens upon dozens of questions which have been asked for almost eight months now would not have led to this situation, had they been answered instead of evaded, or if the minister of northern affairs had risen in his seat, instead of sitting silently, and answered some of the questions asked by the hon. member for Northwest Territories. Yesterday or the day before the hon. member asked in the house whether or not the minister did not give the assurance to the Eskimo people at Fort Chimo that they would be moved at government expense if they did not wish to remain under Quebec jurisdiction. But he sat silent. That is a question which should be answered.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: The question was too ridiculous.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: It is not too ridiculous to the 2,500 people involved.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: And it was not asked.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: The question was asked.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Not of me.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Then why does the minister not answer? Did he give the people of Fort Chimo the assurance that they would be moved at government expense if they did not wish to remain under Quebec jurisdiction?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Of course not, and no Eskimo at Fort Chimo asked me that question.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Then why did you not say so yesterday?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
It seems to me there is a little difference of opinion as to what the council of the Eskimo people at Fort Chimo believe in regard to the assurances given them by the minister, and what the minister believes as being an accurate recollection of the assurances he gave them.

I should like to quote from an article which appeared in the Canada Month for the month of November 1963; I think it will interest the members of the committee and should be on the record.
On page 5 of this publication I find the following:
Eskimo is now the second language of 20 employees of Quebec's bureau of northern planning, reported bureau chief Eric Gourdeau. Only trouble is, the 2,500 Eskimos in northern Quebec are not keen to return the compliment by taking French as their second tongue, asserted northern affairs minister Arthur Laing: Most of their contact has been with English speaking people. Laing's parliamentary assistant, M.P. John Turner, said the Eskimos thought "French" meant "Catholic": "To them the words are synonymous."
Quebec wants to assume responsibility for Eskimos in the province, expects to be able to offer them jobs in coming industrial developments. Ottawa presently administers all Eskimos. Northern affairs Laing insists that, "No discussion will take place without.. .the Eskimo people themselves."
I do not appear to have the article here because I had not planned to take part in this debate-

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Oh, oh.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
I really was not-which
quoted the minister, who I am sure must have read similar articles himself, as giving the assurance to the people of Fort Chimo that financial assistance would be forthcoming to those of the Eskimo people who did not wish to have any part in this transfer.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: I think I might save the hon. member pursuing this matter if I were to tell him that I have a complete tape of every word I uttered there and I would be glad to have him listen to it some time.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
I would be delighted. I only wish that more cabinet ministers might show even that small degree of co-operation to members on this side. I am going to use a term with which I am sure the Minister of Justice is very familiar and which is familiar to a good many people in the country today. It is a basic term in the new dialogue of internal diplomatic expression and I think it is a term which will be understood by the people of Quebec. Within the constitutional framework surely the people of Quebec will understand the right of self-determination.
Recently we have heard a good deal about opting out, such as the opting out that Premier Lesage has done in regard to the Canada pension plan. If he considers this as one of the rights of the province, if he considers this as one of the rights of self-determination within the province of Quebec, then he is one person and his government is one government that will understand the conceding of the right to the Eskimo people to

opt out of this arrangement which the government is considering imposing upon them.
I see that it is five minutes to six, Mr. Chairman, and I am going to take my seat to allow the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources the remaining time before supper to answer some of the questions that have been put to him. I will leave him with one last question about which the Eskimo people at Fort Chimo are very much concerned. If they do wish to opt out, and apparently it seems that they do since 90 to 95 per cent of them do not want anything to do with this transfer, is the government prepared to pay their removal expenses to transport them from the area in which they are now living to other parts of the northland?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I anticipate that most of my remarks on this subject will be made after the dinner hour but I do want to make the comment, in light of the speech made by the Leader of the Opposition, the reply by the Minister of Justice and the intervention of the hon. member for Edmonton West, that it would seem to us who are not members of the bar that for some time to come we are going to live under a government of laws instead of men. I rather think that in the main the calibre of the debate thus far has been quite high-

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Except for Carleton.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
-and while I am quite unable to speak on matters of law I have no intention of degrading the calibre of the debate.
I do want to say that this matter is one that has been before the government of Canada for some time, not only before the present government but before the previous government. My predecessor in this post was approached by officers of the government of Quebec in 1961, I believe, at which time they indicated their interest in taking over the operation of Eskimo affairs in northern Quebec. The tremendous area of Ungava, which was added to the province of Quebec in 1912, is now showing some promise of progress through the development of mines and so on and is thus evoking the interest of more people from southern Canada than it has in the past. According to the count by northern affairs there are about 2,300 Eskimos in the area at the present time located at some 27 posts, with only a very few at some posts, and up to as high as 600 or 700 at the very large posts.
In the couple of minutes left before six o'clock I wish to say that I am extremely proud of the work that northern affairs has done with these people because I would think they are among the most primitive people on the continent, and in many instances the white man has made contact with them for
Supply-Northern Affairs the first time within the last ten years. I am very proud of the work of the officers of the department not only since I have been minister of the department but over the last ten years, during which time contact has been made with these Eskimos.
We are finding that production from their limited resources of fur and fish is increasing greatly. Our officers, particularly in the industrial branch, are bringing along a number of small industries. They are extremely puny in terms of industry in southern Canada, but nevertheless these industries are providing income for the Eskimos.
