I want to tell the committee at this time that there is one place in nouveau Quebec where relief paid in February 1962, amounted to over $8,000, but as a result of developing the resources there and the production of things that the Eskimos can sell the amount of relief paid in February of this year was less than $700.
Mr. Chairman, may I call it six o'clock.
At six o'clock the committee took recess.

AFTER RECESS

The committee resumed at 8 p.m.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
When we adjourned at six o'clock, I had had the opportunity of bringing to the attention of the committee the work which the department of northern affairs has conducted in the northern areas for our Eskimo people over a period of some ten years. I want to say again that I am extremely proud of that work and very happy with the progress that is being made with these people. I want to remind the house that this portion of the responsibility of the department that we are discussing at the present time relates to part of the province of Quebec. There have been indications by the government of Quebec that it would prefer, as the northern sections of that province develop, to take over the administration of the Eskimos in that area.
This proposal has been made not alone to this government but to the previous government as well. We did not decline to discuss the matter with the government of Quebec, and I am quite certain that the previous government did not decline. I am quite certain that my predecessor in this house had discussions with the province of Quebec at that time. They have, on a number of occasions, brought to our attention the fact that they would like to administer the Eskimos in our place. They have asked us if we would enter into discussions with them as to a means by which this could be brought about.
1972	HOUSE OF
Supply-Northern Affairs Now, when these meetings started to take place we immediately had a great number of questions asked in the House of Commons concerning the progress of the discussions.
I think on 16 or 18 different occasions questions have been asked of myself, of the Minister of Justice, of the Prime Minister and various other people. On March 4 I presented to the house a memorandum dealing with the results of a meeting or two we had with officials of the province of Quebec. I gave the house at that time the contents of the memorandum, and I quote:
-is not an agreement, nor is it an agreement to agree. It does constitute a statement outlining a consensus with respect to certain basic principles and conditions which, in the event of an agreement, are common to the two governments.
I went on to list these various conditions, four in all, as found on page 506 of Hansard tor March 4. The questions that have arisen in the house have dealt largely with the matter of consultation. There was a prolonged series of questions on March 10, which ended in an exchange between the Prime Minister and the Leader of the Opposition. The Prime Minister, as recorded on page 736 of Hansard, said this:
If it will prevent a further waste of time by additional questions, I will say once again that the Eskimos will be consulted before an agreement is signed.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Full retreat.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: I cannot allow the last remark made by the Prime Minister to pass unchallenged. We on this side of the house have at last been able to get an answer indicating that these primitive people-

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Oh, oh.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: -are not going to be treated as chattels by this government.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: On the point of order, if the right hon. gentleman would read Hansard he will find this question specifically answered by the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources days ago. I suggest he read the statement.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
No, no. We got the answer today.
Well, I would interpret the words of the Leader of the Opposition to mean that at long last he was satisfied he had gotten an answer. A few days later, when I was on government business in the province of British Columbia, a series of questions were asked again by the hon. member for Yukon. They were directed to my parliamentary secretary who provided some answers and then said that any further replies would have to await my return. I returned to the House of Commons a day or two after this, but no questions were asked of me then.
However, later we came to this point just a matter of a few days ago, on April 6, when the hon. member for Peace River dealt with it. He tried to establish in the minds of members of the house that there had been a 

fait accompli; everything was cut and dried. The hon. member said, as recorded on page
1839 of Hansard for that date:
It has been admitted in the house that this transfer is going to take place.
Some time later I intervened to ask him if he would refer me to the page in Hansard where that quotation was made. The hon. member said he was sure his seatmate would be glad to look this up while he was proceeding with his remarks. The hon. member's seatmate was the hon. member for Yukon.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: He is going to get it now.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: He has had since April 6 to find it. I do not think he will find it because it was never made in the House of Commons. This was the general buildup.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
May I draw the minister's attention to page 506 of Hansard, the statement to which he has already referred, where he set forth the consensus. He will find, in the left hand column, about half way down the page where he said:
Canada is prepared to have Quebec administer Eskimo affairs as part of Quebec's general administrative responsibilities in the province.
Surely that constitutes an assurance that the transfer is going to be made?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: I think I read the preface to my statement which said this is not an agreement or even an agreement to agree. How the hon. member can read that statement, and interpret it to mean that it was admitted in the house that this transfer was going to be made, is beyond my comprehension.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
Surely the minister will agree with me the meaning of his words was quite clear and when he said:
Canada is prepared to have Quebec administer Eskimo affairs as part of Quebec's general administrative responsibilities in the province.
Does the minister not agree that what he is saying there in effect is that the federal government is prepared to transfer the administrative responsibilities over Eskimos in the province of Quebec to the province of Quebec?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
At the beginning of page 505,
as I have already stated. I said the memorandum was not an agreement, nor an agreement to agree, which was a preface to the entire statement. All we were doing was setting out a few basic principles by which we would be guided in any negotiations we had with the province of Quebec.
I am a little bit concerned that the hon. member for Yukon thinks if he can make an assertion in the committee that is not denied, then he clothes it with veracity. I can assure him that is not the case at all. We have

been sitting here listening to these repeated questions inferring that an agreement has been completed, and in the absence of a complete denial each time I think now some hon. members opposite are beginning to believe their own words. I think it was an American humorist named Josh Billings who took care of this situation, when he said: "It ain't the things a man don't know that makes him look foolish, but the things he does know that ain't so." I think there are a number of things hon. members on the opposite side have believed are so, but are not so.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: On that basis is the minister prepared to indicate now, with reasonable assurance, that no transfer will take place?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
The hon. member has asked me a question, and I intend to deal with the matter as I go along. I want to direct this to the attention of members of the committee, that in the arrangement of these affairs dealing with our indigenous people I would think it would be a natural thing for a national government, as time goes on and as conditions warrant it, to work closely with provincial governments in the supply of services to these people.
I want to pay some attention to what I thought was a very fine argument made last week in this regard by the hon. member for Skeena, that it is unthinkable that forever we should have two classes of people. Certain hon. members opposite are laughing. They are people who apparently would believe that it is good to keep people on two levels perpetually, and they are not prepared to agree or admit that a province is capable of rendering services equivalent to those given by a national government. With that I cannot agree.
I want to draw the attention of the committee to a statement made in the house on April 8, 1960, by a former minister of citizenship and immigration, the Hon. Ellen Fair-clough. As recorded at page 3037 of Hansard for that date, she said this:
Second, I wish to announce that the federal government is prepared to negotiate agreements with the governments of the various provinces for the extension of normal provincial welfare services to persons residing on Indian reserves.
Now, as hon. members know, section 113 of the Indian Act provides for these agreements in respect to educational matters only, but here in 1960 the previous government announced as a policy of that government that it was prepared to extend these agreements with the provinces to welfare services.
She continued:
The purpose is to avoid the development of exclusive welfare services on reserves which would
Supply-Northern Affairs
tend to set Indians apart from other Canadians and duplicate provincial programs in adjacent nonIndian communities.
In negotiating these agreements the federal government is prepared to pay a reasonable share of the costs of the benefits, over and above the federal contribution under existing federal-provincial agreements, such as the Unemployment Assistance Act; and to share with the provinces reasonable costs of additional staff and administration required for the application of such programs. Moreover, my department will be prepared to enter into agreements to enable Indian bands to assume responsibilities for welfare programs normally administered by municipalities under provincial legislation.
Today we had the right hon. Leader of the Opposition attacking us for negotiating with the provinces when, under his own leadership, his government had announced in 1960 that it was prepared specifically to do those things.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Could the minister deal with the exception made in section 4 of the Indian Act, which specifically excludes Eskimos from the operation of that act?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
Well, I think I have dealt fairly adequately with the attitude of the right hon. Leader of the Opposition today, as compared with the statement made on behalf of his government on April 8, 1960.
In addition, I want to point out that in my riding of Vancouver South, which is a purely urban riding that contains some of the largest homes in the city, there is an Indian reserve of some 600 or 700 acres, the Musqueam Indian reserve. About four or five years ago, when the right hon. gentleman who sits opposite was prime minister, an agreement was made at that time under the pressure of the then chief, who happened to be an Indian woman named Mrs. Guerin, to have the children from that reserve not attend the little school on the reserve but to go to the Kerrisdale school with white pupils. She had to fight a long battle with the Vancouver school board and with some of the parents of the area. I have kept a watch on developments since, and I wish to say it proved again that in this world there are no indigenously inferior people. Those children are coming along just as well as any white child in the school.
This integration, if you want to call it that, this understanding between whites and indigenous people, is a thing all governments should support so long as it can be adequately done and safeguards provided.
I am now going to draw the attention of the committee to the fact that the hon. member for Skeena has been consistent in this regard, because immediately after that announcement was made by the minister in 1960 he said, as recorded at the same page of Hansard:

Supply-Northern Affairs
We also appreciate the announcements made by the minister with respect to these two matters, which are exceptionally good ones. We hope additional steps will be taken later on in order to deal with other similar problems.
That is, dealing with the problem of bringing welfare matters more closely under the direction of those governments that were on the ground, rather than under the central government. Therefore, I think any claim that exception should be taken to administration of these schemes by the provincial government is not sound, is not historically correct, and probably would have been the policy of the previous government as well.
I want to tell the committee some of the things that occurred on an exceptional trip I took last summer over some 7,000 miles of the northern territory, during which we held a couple of gatherings of the Quebec Eskimo people, first at Fort Chimo and second at Great Whale River. This is language taken from an interpreter. It is not particularly erudite language but I want to give the committee some of the remarks I made to the Eskimo elders when we met them at Fort Chimo on September 10, 1963.
Getting down to the present situation, I can understand it if the Eskimos find it hard to explain that one government should argue with another government that it can do better by him. We are dealing with a moral responsibility. And since it is a moral responsibility, the first primary, predominant consideration is the person that we are trying to help. In other words, the Eskimos. And the government of Canada has accepted this moral responsibility. Accepting this moral responsibility does not mean that we shall exclude other agencies or other governments from giving assistance to Eskimos. This is part of Canada but this is also the province of Quebec. And there are provincial laws which have to do with people over which the federal government has no control and an area which it does not invade. We white people make a statement now and again that we prefer the devil we know to the devil we do not know. I think in the minds of some of the people here there is that feeling. Most of the concern, I think, about the administration of Quebec-because this is Quebec and the Quebec government has to administer this area in respect of a number of things-I think most of the concern has to do with exercising the sanction of the game laws. I cannot believe that they would impose white man's game laws on Indians and Eskimos.
Now then, when we get down to talk of takeover, there have been two discussions in which I was involved with officials of the province of Quebec. They were initiated by the province of Quebec. They asked for the discussions. There have been no negotiations whatsoever in respect of a takeover. In other words, the operation of northern affairs in respect to assisting Eskimos in various ways is in the identical position today as it was two years ago. If there are any further discussions which could lead to negotiations, I am going to propose to the people of Quebec, the representatives of the government of Quebec, that no action be taken without consulting the Eskimo people themselves and I do that because the only interest in our being here and spending a tremendous sum of money here is the good of the Eskimo people themselves.
[Mr. Laing.3

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Would the hon. member permit a question? Did any of the Eskimo leaders say to the minister at any time during his visit to Fort Chimo last September, or did they indicate to him either in English or through interpreters, that they did not want their affairs transferred to the province of Quebec?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Of course I have just read my statement, I could read another-

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: I want to know what the Eskimos said to the minister, not what he said to them.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: I could read the entire account. I had heard representations from the Eskimo people and this was my reply.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: I was looking for a simple answer-yes, or no. Did any of the Eskimo people at that time indicate that they did not want their affairs transferred? Surely a simple yes or no could be given; I do not want the transcript of what was said.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Of course some Eskimos said they were fearful of any transfer. Most of them said they were extremely happy with the administration of affairs by the department of northern affairs. I have made that statement on a number of occasions. As a matter of fact, I did so when I returned. The hon. member has no need to ask that question in the committee, now.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
Would the minister permit me to intervene for a moment? During the dinner hour I have been able to find the press reports to which I referred earlier in my remarks before the recess. This is an article by Mr. Dafoe which appeared in the Winnipeg Free Press.
The Eskimo council met with federal northern affairs minister Arthur Laing to express their concern about the transfer of authority and asked for federal assistance in moving out of the province if Quebec did get control.
I wonder if the minister could tell us whether any such offer of federal financial assistance was made at the time of his visit.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: This is another case of the hon. member taking up a statement which appeared in the press and trying to establish it as a fact in the house.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Well, I am asking the minister.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
No single Eskimo made any suggestion to me with regard to our providing transport or accommodation for him to leave the territory. That has been said before. A number of meetings have been held with the province of Quebec, and the differences which exist between us principally have to do with what is meant by consultation.

I want to tell the committee now that the position I have taken, the position we have taken, in respect to what "consultation" means, this being the outcome of the memorandum I gave to the house on March 4-and nothing has been concluded or undertaken by us or by the Quebec government since, and as a result of that memorandum-our interpretation of the meaning of "consultation", the position we are taking now is that we would not exclude from the consultation with the Eskimos any aspect of the proposed arrangement with Quebec for the provision of those services. This confirms what I said both at Fort Chimo and at Great Whale River and represents the continuing attitude of the government.
The Leader of the Opposition asked three specific questions this afternoon. He asked whether an agreement had been concluded. He asked whether a proposal had been put up that we pay 50 per cent, or 100 per cent of the cost. I want to assure the committee that at this moment no agreement has been reached with Quebec in any respect whatsoever. My officials are dealing with officials of the Quebec government with respect to putting into effect, or working from, that memorandum presented to the house on March 4, and that is where the matter stands.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
Before the minister concludes, I wonder if I might ask him one question bearing on the remarks he made as to his interpretation of what "consultation" means. Frankly, I agree with him that that is what consultation should mean. But from what he has said it would appear there has been no consultation with the Eskimo people themselves with regard to the provisions, the terms of the consensus which he read into the record on March 4.
I should like the hon. gentleman to assure us that there has been consultation with respect to the provisions of the consensus between the two governments. The minister said that since March 4 there have been continuing conversations between officials of his department and those of the government of Quebec. Have the Eskimo people been represented with regard to those conversations?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
Of course, Mr. Chairman, in the light of the memorandum which I brought to the house, how could they be expected to? The memorandum was a memorandum of a set of principles which, in our view, were prerequisite to our accomplishing anything by way of an agreement with Quebec, and we are still in a state of argument, if you like, on the question of what constitutes consultation with the province of Quebec. Certainly that is the primary step, one which must be
Supply-Northern Affairs taken prior to any discussion with the Eskimos. As far as consultation is concerned, I am having a consultation with my hon. friend from Yukon and I am quite certain that every time I sit down he will make his views known to me. I think that is consultation, and that is the attitude we are taking in this matter.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I wonder
whether the minister will give this committee his assurance that on the commission to be set up between the two governments, if indeed the government insists upon going ahead with this unconstitutional plan after having heard these arguments, he will have representatives of the Eskimo council, or independent counsel obtained by the Eskimo people, who will be sitting on the commission and taking part in the discussions as to the provisions of any eventual agreement?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, this aspect has been discussed by my officials and the officials of the government of Quebec.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: I am very glad to hear that the matter has been discussed by the officials of the two governments, but my question was: Will the minister assure us that the Eskimo people, through a representative of their council or by independent counsel selected by them, will be represented on that commission? Will the minister answer that question for us?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: The hon. member for Edmonton West.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I would like to ask the minister to either rise and give us that assurance or tell us he cannot give us that assurance-one way or the other; because I am sure we are all interested in finding out whether the government intends to have the Eskimo people represented at all on that commission. Surely we are entitled to an answer.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I was trying to establish some more facts for my hon. friend by not giving a denial. We certainly will see to it, because of the construction we put upon "consultation", that the views of the Eskimos are known by whatever means we can obtain them.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
I am afraid, Mr. Chairman, I still have to ask the minister whether he will be kind enough to consider the question I have asked him. It is a very simple question: Will he either give the committee his assurance, or not give the committee his assurance, that the Eskimo people will be represented on the commission either by someone of their council or by independent counsel selected by them? This is the assurance that we want.

Supply-Northern Affairs

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: We will consider that, Mr. Chairman.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I wonder whether the minister could deal with those points which I raised with his colleague the Minister of Justice. The Minister of Justice assured me that the Minister of Northern Affair and National Resources would deal with them. They deal with who shall have the say on the norms for education, and whether there shall be any independence or discretion as to policy on the basis of agency, as it has been indicated that any agreement will be on the basis of principal and agent.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: There has been no consultation between the ministers.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Certainly in any discussions we have had with Quebec, and in our own minds, the maintenance of the present standards of service would be prerequisite to any arrangement at all; and not only maintenance but an extension of those services, because not in all districts have we the full grades of education that are going to be soon required in the area; we have school to grades 4 and 5 in some places. In addition to that we have not secured all the children in the area, but about 65 per cent, for the schools. So the standards we would insist upon would have to be as good as those we have now and, in addition, would have to take care of the future requirements of the population.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: This is what I am concerned with, in that the level of the educational facilities will be comparable in the ultimate evolution of the educational process in the area with, say, the Eskimos in the western Arctic. Will this be the case?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Quite obviously they will have to be. We are somewhat behind, in that area, in the provision of schools, partly because of the discussions that have taken place. I think we are prepared this year, in respect of Chimo, to put a $300,000 school there.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, may I ask the minister just how he expects to make the province comply with federal requirements in this matter of education?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: The hon. member for Bran-don-Souris.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, the minister just gave an answer and I think he would want to clarify that answer by answering the question I have asked.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
Of course, Mr. Chairman, education being one of the prime considerations, it would be included in the agreement. I am quite certain the hon. member would not 
wish to suggest that either we or a province, having entered into such an agreement, would show bad faith thereafter. The standards would be maintained as under the agreement, of course.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: There is no suggestion of that. I just wanted to know how the federal government can exercise its control in the matter of education to see that the school facilities and standards are equivalent to those now in force. The minister has not answered that question to my satisfaction.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: The hon. member for Bran-don-Souris.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Mr. Chairman-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Perhaps the hon. member will have an opportunity to make a contribution and ask questions after a while. It seems to me we will make better progress that way.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: On a point of order, Mr. Chairman, I think that for intelligent discussion, if the minister is replying to a question he should reply to it fully so that we will not have to come back again on that particular point. My question is absolutely pertinent to the point raised by the hon. member who asked the previous question.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Surely, Mr. Chairman, my hon. friend does not suggest that the province of Quebec would not wish to maintain the standards.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: I am not suggesting anything. I am asking the minister a question, and he persists in not answering it.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Arrogance.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: You are looking at yourself in a mirror.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: My hon. friend did not deal with the language question at all, though he probably inferred that. He dealt with the quality of education. If Quebec agrees to maintain a certain quality of education, is he suggesting they are going to fall down on that agreement?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: That is not the answer to my question, Mr. Chairman; it is another question.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: I recognize the hon. member for Brandon-Souris.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
Thank you, Mr. Chairman. The item under which we are carrying out this interesting discussion is vote le, which concerns itself largely with a grant to the Canadian council of resource ministers. 1 think it is most appropriate that we are having this particular discussion under this

vote, because the hon. minister has already intimated that there were some discussions on this subject in which I, as the minister of northern affairs and national resources in the former administration, took part. On both these occasions the discussions were incidental to the subject of the resource ministers council. As a matter of fact, the first time I was approached on the subject was during the course of the very successful resources for tomorrow conference in the city of Montreal in October, 1961.
On that occasion the minister of natural resources for the province of Quebec incidentally referred to his government's interest in the matter of administering the affairs of the Eskimos of new Quebec. The second occasion on which the subject was raised was also a meeting following the resources conference, a meeting at which we were making the final arrangements for bringing into effect on a permanent basis the resource ministers council, and again this subject was raised incidentally.
Realizing the constitutional importance of the supreme court's decision of 1939-I am not getting into the constitutional aspects tonight because I feel this has been quite adequately dealt with by my legal confreres on this side of the house-I suggested to the minister of resources for the province of Quebec that it was of such vital and fundamental importance that it should be discussed at the highest levels, namely by the prime ministers of the two governments concerned. The last contact I recall having had on this subject was on March 16, 1963 when I replied to the minister of resources, who was inquiring when the premier of the province of Quebec might hear from the Prime Minister of Canada. In reply to the remarks of the minister tonight with reference to any negotiations which the former administration might have had, I have to indicate that this is all that transpired. In other words, we stood firm on the constitutional aspects of this problem.
There is another reason for my entering the discussion at this time. This is the first opportunity that I have had to refer to the passing of one of the senior officials of the department of northern affairs. I refer to the late Frank Cunningham, who was the assistant deputy minister for a number of years and one of the men who played a key role in implementing many of the progressive policies which have taken place in northern development during the past five or six years. Mr. Frank Cunningham retired early because of ill health and did not live many months beyond his retirement. I am sure the minister of northern affairs would join me in indicating that he was the type of devoted civil
Supply-Northern Affairs servant in the department of northern affairs to which the minister referred in opening his remarks tonight. Mr. Cunningham was largely concerned with roads to resources and the material aspects of the northern development program.
This brings me to the point that I want to present to the committee tonight. All the policies which were implemented by the former administration with respect to northern development our primary concern was with the development of human resources. The minister agrees with this viewpoint, and has indicated this is so in the remarks he has made to the committee tonight. The only reason I am speaking at this time is because as I listened to him I saw a ray of hope that the door was still open, and that he is not yet firmly convinced that the step being contemplated by the present government, namely the transfer of administration and jurisdiction of the Eskimos of northern Quebec to the provincial government, will be in the best interests of these people. As a matter of fact, I think the case could be proven that this might indeed be a retrograde step.
The minister paid high tribute to the work that has been carried out by the department of northern affairs in all parts of northern Canada. Having said that, he then indicated he is willing to transfer the jurisdiction and administration of this territory to another level of government. I am sure all members of this committee will agree that the record of Canada and the governments of Canada with reference to the original Canadians- the first Canadians as they are sometimes called-is not a good one. I am not going to recite the long sad story of governmental neglect in the area of both Indian affairs and Eskimo affairs. The problem has been confounded by the sort of paternalism which completely ignores the wishes of the people concerned with regard to the administration of their own affairs, as contemplated by this transfer of jurisdiction. I could speak of the neglect in the areas of health, the problems which have been compounded by segregation on reserves, by educational segregation, and so forth and so on. It is only in recent years that both the Indian affairs branch and the department of northern affairs have moved forward with a progressive policy toward our first Canadians.
As a result of the improved health program the Indians and Eskimos are no longer a vanishing people. The infant mortality rate was of shockingly high proportions until the department of northern affairs and the northern health services branch moved into this area of Canadian activity. Educational

Supply-Northern Affairs programs were one of the keystones of northern development under the former administration. It should be pointed out that the first program for sponsored university education in any part of Canada was undertaken on behalf of the citizens of northern Canada by the department of northern affairs. Then the great leap forward with respect to our first Canadians was the granting of the franchise, the unrestricted franchise. This was the first genuine indication that the government of Canada was concerned in moving these people forward from third to second class citizenship to first class citizenship.
A great deal of interest has been generated in the major metropolitan press across the country with regard to this question. Top flight reporters have been sent into the area concerned to examine the problem at the grassroots level. I have been disturbed to find comments of the politicians concerned which seem to suggest that these first Canadians, our original Canadians, are a backward people. This has been the case with some of the public figures in the province of Quebec involved in these discussions. As a matter of fact the minister of resources of the province of Quebec has repeatedly indicated that he is willing to consult in all aspects of this problem except the fundamental area, the matter of the transfer of administration and jurisdiction. One of the most disturbing statements came from the M.L.A. who represents this area of northern Quebec, who demanded that the franchise should be removed from these northern Quebec Eskimos. This is why I feel there is a strong possibility that the step contemplated might be a retrograde one.
The minister has indicated his confidence in the capacity of these northern citizens. I can confirm this on the basis of the many contacts I have made. For example, Fort Chimo is one of the main communities concerned, and the Fort Chimo Eskimo cooperative is one of the most progressive of all northern co-operatives at present in operation. I recall a press conference that was held at the Ottawa press club in August of 1962 when representatives of the Fort Chimo co-operative came to Ottawa to promote the sale of Arctic char. They were exposed to a full battery of questions on the part of members of the parliamentary press gallery, and their answers were so sophisticated and competent that one press interrogator suggested that the Eskimos had been briefed. He said to one of them: "You sit there and you answer these questions with all the sophistication of a business executive". The Eskimo could not speak English, but speaking through an interpreter he said: "If I look like a business executive it is because
[Mr. DinsdaleJ

I am a business executive; I am president of the Fort Chimo Eskimo co-operative".
Very often the uninitiated, those who are unfamiliar with these excellent people, refer to them as backward, not ready for the franchise and not capable of handling their own affairs as other Canadians do. I could refer to the first conference of Eskimo cooperatives held at Frobisher Bay just a year ago, when representatives from right across the Arctic as well as northern Quebec met at Frobisher Bay for a conference which lasted several days. They carried on discussion in an economic conference that would compare favourably with many of the conferences that are conducted in the southern parts of Canada.
I am giving a friendly warning to my successor, the present minister, that every indication in the house up to the present time concerning this move would suggest that the government is moving in a retrograde direction. The new government has repeatedly given lip service to a more humanitarian and enlightened approach to the problems of our first Canadians. This is the first major action that the government has contemplated and it threatens to reverse all the gains that have been made in recent years by their predecessors in governmental responsibility.
I am going to make four recommendations that should be taken into consideration by the government as they contemplate this problem. I think it has been proven beyond any shadow of doubt in the discussion today that before there can be any change of jurisdiction a constitutional amendment is required. This is a national problem. It is one that applies to both Indians and Eskimos and it concerns all the provinces. If we are going to continue as a federal state we cannot deal with this problem only within the jurisdictional area of one province. We must consider the entire national perspective. Yet the minister has already indicated that the government is willing to negotiate notwithstanding the constitutional prerequisite.
My colleague, the hon. member for Pontiac-Temiscamingue, stated the constitutional position quite precisely the other day, I thought, when he made his excellent contribution to this discussion. I noticed that when the hon. member for Carleton tried to deal with this matter without any reference to authorities he did not refer to the excellent contribution of the hon. member for Pontiac-Temisca-mingue who presented the Quebec viewpoint on this matter. Rather he dealt with the questions that had been propounded by the hon. member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm who has not yet made a speech on this subject. I suggest that the hon. member for Carleton

should follow the lead that has been given by the hon. member for Pontiac-Temisca-mingue.
The second recommendation I wish to make to the minister and the government is that the wishes of the Eskimos be respected in these matters. So far as I have been able to determine, the Eskimos have made no requests for this jurisdictional transfer. If there is one fundamental principle that is more important than another it is the fundamental right of self-determination, which Canada has insisted upon in discussions at the United Nations and other international gatherings, with regard to the treatment of other peoples who have not yet assumed the full status and quality of citizenship. This is a basic human right and I think the minister would be well advised to take this into consideration. There has been no agitation by the Eskimos for this transfer. On the other hand, in every case where the Indians have been granted certain concessions requests have come from the Indians themselves in each instance.
Mr. McTaggart, the former principal of the school at Fort Chimo, has got into the public discussion recently. I know Mr. McTaggart. He comes from the province of Manitoba and I am sure that Manitobans are noted for their-

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
Perhaps the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre might help me- tolerance and temperance in these matters. The point Mr. McTaggart was trying to make was that the wishes of the people of Fort Chimo were being ignored. It may be that he trespassed, so far as his responsibilities as a civil servant are concerned, but I do not think it can be denied that he had a legitimate point in trying to present the body of public opinion in this northern community as he understood it.
The next point I should like to make is that the discussions must include both Eskimos and Indians. Otherwise we will have discrimination between these two groups of first Canadians. I simply refer to the situation at Great Whale River where you have Indians and Eskimos living side by side. If the Eskimos are under one jurisdiction and the Indians under another jurisdiction you will have segregation and confusion confounded. The first native Indian to serve in this parliament-I refer to Senator Gladstone-has made the point repeatedly that the problems of these two peoples cannot be considered in isolation. They are one and the same and indivisible. As a matter of fact, he has repeatedly recommended that both these groups should be brought under the jurisdiction of one department and he prefers the 20220-125
Supply-Northern Affairs Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources because of the excellent record they have established in administering the affairs of the Eskimos.

speakerposition: Minister of Amateur Sport; Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: The Eskimos are no more Indian than is Senator Gladstone.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: My hon. friend the minister of health and welfare says the Eskimos are no more Indians than is Senator Gladstone.

speakerposition: Minister of Amateur Sport; Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Except legally.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
The minister should read the decision of the supreme court in 1939 in this respect.
The final point I should like to make, Mr. Chairman, is that parliament must decide this issue. This is the reason for the extended discussion on these estimates. This matter must be brought before parliament because it is a fundamental issue of human rights and only parliament, not the government, is qualified and has authority to deal with it.
Before concluding, I should like to make one or two additional points. The Minister of Justice maintains that this whole matter is administrative. I want to ask him how you can turn over administration without affecting the jurisdiction? How can you enter upon such matters as health of the Eskimos, medical care, schools, welfare and justice, without possessing jurisdictional authority to do so? If this is the case, then this government is either being false to Quebec or false to the constitution.
If Quebec has a legitimate claim, and no member on this side of the house has said it has not, then the proper constitutional steps must be taken to turn over jurisdiction. The hon. member for Pontiac-Temiscamingue made this fundamental point. This is not the first time that this government has tried to cut corners. It has done it in so many other basic matters in this house in recent months. The government, for some reason, is trying to approach this matter in an underhanded, devious and uncertain manner. It is for this reason we on this side of the house are objecting. Our objection is to this government's total incapacity to act in accordance with the principle that a straight line is the shortest distance between two points.
The confusion that has resulted has been caused directly by the government's devious methods. There is no need for unseemly haste. Certainly, Mr. Chairman, there is no need for unparliamentary haste in dealing with this fundamental issue.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
We dealt with this same subject on another occasion, and while it is of vital importance because it affects the rights of people, nevertheless I do not think

Supply-Northern Affairs it warrants the extensive repetition that has taken place, certainly not in so far as I am concerned. However, listening to the minister explain the situation this evening, particularly when he answered questions posed by members of the Conservative party, he left a distinct impression with me that he had something to hide; that he was in a box and that he was trying to explain away an awkward situation. This is regrettable. I think perhaps the minister is in a situation, unfortunately, not entirely of his own making and he is making the best of a bad job.
I do not know who initiated these discussions, but I think it would be the province of Quebec. I think it is quite obvious, after listening to the hon. member from Brandon-Souris, that the discussion of the transfer of jurisdiction really did start at the ministerial level. There was not any concern on the part of the government of Quebec or on the part of this government, in attempting to discover the attitude of the people themselves. I believe this is what the minister is trying to cover up, and it is a regrettable situation. I gather it is not only the Liberal government that is responsible for this sort of high level bungling, or attempts at high levels to deal with the rights of people. I say that because of the admission made by the hon. member for Brandon-Souris just a moment ago. He was attending the resources for tomorrow conference in Quebec and was approached on this question. His answer was that this matter should be discussed at the highest level, and he qualified that by referring to the level of the Prime Minister of Canada and the premier of Quebec.
This is where the error was made in the first instance. What the hon. member for Brandon-Souris should have said on that occasion, if his words now mean anything or reflect the attitude of his party, was that this matter should be discussed at the highest level, namely, the level of the people concerned. This is the only level at which it should be discussed. I have tried to make this point time and time again with the minister: When you are dealing with the rights of people, for heaven's sake consult these people first. If you do not do that, you have no business proceeding further with any discussion, developing memoranda or answering letters. In this instance, the Eskimo people should have been consulted first to ascertain what they wanted. Then the minister, as the one responsible for their affairs, should be their representative, and negotiate for them. You do not consummate an agreement, then come back and try to sell it to the native people. So far as I am concerned you should discontinue these discussions with Quebec until you

find out what the Eskimo people themselves want, and you should not do anything else.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Would the hon. member permit a question?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: He has indicated that the initial error was the suggestion the matter should be discussed at the highest level, the prime minister's level. Does he not recall that one of the points I made during my observations tonight was that no discussion ever took place at that level, and my stand was that you must consult with the people concerned.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: The hon. member also said he suggested it should be discussed at the highest level, and he referred to the level of the Prime Minister and the premier of Quebec. He can qualify that by using the phrase he has just used now, but the fact is that he made that statement and did that.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, several days ago we were discussing this subject and I raised a few points. Until that time I had refrained from entering the debate, even though as a resident of the Northwest Territories and as the member representing the bulk of the Eskimo people in this country, I am quite prepared to stand in this house and tell the Prime Minister, the Minister of Justice and the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources a few things about the Eskimo people that they may not know. However, I participate at this point because I have not had answers to the basic issues I raised.
By way of comment, I was fascinated by a headline in tonight's Ottawa Citizen, which 1 assume came from the pen of the Prime Minister's nephew, who is editor of that paper, in which he says the Prime Minister is going to the country if there is any more delay in the house. I say to the Prime Minister and to the committee, we would love to go to the country on the issue of whether or not 2,500 Canadian people are going to be pushed around. I will gladly campaign anywhere, from one end of the country to the other, on that very issue.
Until we get some answers I am quite prepared to talk, and talk, and talk. I say to any of the brave gentlemen opposite, with their northern experience, like the hon. member for Carleton, who want to tell us something about the north, let them stand up and I will gladly take my seat while they pose their questions.
I want to say to the minister I have confidence in the stand he has taken within the cabinet on this matter. I have confidence in the kind of things he told the Eskimo people

on his visit to the Canadian north last fall. My recollection is that just before he went to Fort Chimo he bumped into me in the Canadian Arctic and I suggested to him, having come from Fort Chimo myself, that he might run into this problem. I know the Eskimo people at Chimo have a reasonable degree of confidence in him, but I am not confident in the things the Minister of Justice said in the committee today, because I am satisfied he is the one who has the power in this play going on between the federal government and the provincial government.
The Minister of Justice said today, "Don't worry, whatever is best for the people shall be done," but I say to him nearly all of the unpleasant, unsavoury, unacceptable and unworthy things that happened to me in my life have happened to me at the hands of people who were doing what was best for me, and I am not prepared to have the Minister of Justice decide what is best for me and what is best for 2,500 Canadian citizens who happen to be Eskimos in northern Quebec.
There are a few issues which I have raised in the house and I intend to raise them again in the committee tonight. One important issue that has been the curse of many previous ministers of northern affairs is whether the people of the Canadian north are going to be consulted about major policy matters or not? This is the issue.
The people of the north are a special kind of people. The minister who represents them in parliament-and I must say I am happy with the way the present minister is representing us who live in the north-must have a special kind of courage. He must have a special understanding of what we, who choose to live in the Canadian north, want. We insist on being consulted before things like this happen. It may have been good enough in previous years for the federal government and the House of Commons to do things to the Canadian north, but it is no longer good enough, and so far as I am concerned, so long as I am its member, I shall take this same position on every issue that is raised. You are going to consult us, Mr. Minister, before you decide what you are going to do with our lives.
I want to draw the attention of the committee to the fact that in Ottawa at the present time we have gathered together a group of our northern officials in conference. They are here to give the minister and his senior officials the benefit of the experience they have had over the past two years. Every two years the department brings these men and women from all parts of Canada in to Ottawa, and I say to the minister if he wants to find out what is going on, let him consult these people. They are all here, brought to 20220-125J
Supply-Northern Affairs Ottawa at considerable expense to the taxpayer, and surely no one begrudges the cost of that. For goodness sake, I say to the minister, talk to them. He has all his officers here from northern Quebec. Let him ask them what are the issues at stake right now. Let him go to these people and find out.
My hon. friend suggests a deal has been made. I am not sure it has. Hopefully, I suggest it has not. The reason I am speaking now is because questions I raised several weeks ago were not answered. Indeed, it was not until this afternoon that the minister got up and, under tremendous pressure from the hon. member for Yukon, finally admitted that several people, several Eskimo people, had told him they were opposed to the transfer of their affairs to the jurisdiction of the Quebec government. Why in the world could he not have said that in the house two days ago? I asked him whether the people of northern Quebec suggested to him that they did not want to be administered by Quebec. I asked him whether any of them had asked him about getting help to move to the Northwest Territories. He sat there and said nothing.
It was only today, when finally a minister of the crown realized his estimates might not get through until he was prepared to level with the committee and the people of Canada, that he got up to speak. There has been a lot of talk about consulting the Eskimo people. How do you consult with the Eskimo people? I will tell you how to do it. I am waiting for a definitive statement to be made on this matter by the hon. member for Saguenay, who represents the Eskimo people. During the dinner recess, out of curiosity, 1 looked up the last poll results from the northern Eskimo settlements in Quebec. 1 was not happy with them, but I was interested to learn that they voted almost solidly in favour of the hon. member for Saguenay, who happens to be on the government side of the house.
Apparently we are not afraid to consult those people when we want them to elect a member of parliament from northern Quebec. I know the way the last election was fought. Apparently we did not hesitate to take the issues of nuclear weapons, cabinet solidarity and balance of payments to the Eskimo people in the north when they voted for the hon. member for Saguenay, but all of a sudden they are not competent to say whether or not their affairs should be administered by the provincial government. I suggest it is a glaring omission that the hon. member for Saguenay has yet to make a single statement in the committee.
If he is not prepared to speak for the 2,500 Eskimo people in northern Quebec, then by

Supply-Northern Affairs default I am prepared to speak for them. I am prepared to say to the minister that I am not satisfied with the reasons given for the negotiations and dealings made to date. I am satisfied that this is nothing more than an exercise in political appeasement to the province of Quebec, and I am prepared to continue talking in the committee to see to it that we get to the bottom of the issue.
One of the chief negotiators in this matter has been the minister of resources in the province of Quebec. The Minister of Justice assures us, turn these people over to Quebec and all shall be well. Yet this same minister, Hon. Rene Levesque, says it will be an abuse of democracy to give the Eskimo people the right to vote on it. He says it is hypocrisy; that those who want this vote are hypocrites. I ask, should the Canadian people entrust the affairs of our Eskimo people to this kind of person who is prepared to make this kind of statement?
I want the minister to reassure me on this matter. I want him to reassure the Eskimo people. He can reassure me tonight by clearing up the one or two areas that are still in doubt. Further, I want him to do something else, and I am really prepared to help him.
I want him to write a letter to the Eskimo people of northern Quebec. I have all their names and addresses. I have a typewriter that will type in syllables. My secretary is an Eskimo and she will help with the translation. I want him to do this while we in southern Canada are tussling over the question of the administration of Eskimo affairs. I want him to write a letter and give to them the same kind of reassurance that hopefully he has given us.
Write them a letter. Tell them that he is their minister. Tell them that they can count on the trust they have in him-and I know they have trust in him. Write them a letter. I will help him print it. He can use my typewriter. Let him say that while we southern Canadians are fighting over this issue they need not worry because he will see to it that their constitutional rights and their right to self-determination will be defended, just as would be the rights of any other Canadians. That is what I am asking him to do tonight.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
I do not intend to deal with the legal and constitutional aspects of the matter before us. I feel that the Minister of Justice has dealt well and capably with them. I do wish to refer to certain aspects of the speech made by the hon. member for Yukon who tried throughout the course of his address this evening, as, indeed, he did in his earlier interventions on this subject, to put words into the mouth of the minister of northern affairs.

The hon. member is a lawyer with experience in a tough territory where life is harder than it is in southern Canada. He has had experience before the courts. Versed as he is in the common law, after many years of practice he knows it is an old and respected principle of the common law that silence is never to be equated with acquiescence or acquiescence deemed to follow necessarily from silence. Yet, this evening, having in mind the fact that over the past several weeks questions have been posed by hon. members of his party, some of which have not been answered by the minister, either because-[DOT] with respect, Mr. Chairman-they were out of order, or inflammatory, or hypothetical, or argumentative, because the minister has not chosen to abuse the rules of the house in the same fashion, his silence is interpreted by the hon. member for Yukon as acquiescence. I put it to the hon. member that he is too accomplished a lawyer to believe in that principle, though from time to time he is too enthusiastic a debater to follow it.
1 want to suggest to the committee that what the member for the Yukon has tried to do with the statement made by my minister, the minister of northern affairs to the House of Commons on March 4 is this: misread it, misinterpret it, colour it by omission, and separate the preface from the integral part of the statement, though the preface is an important part of that statement. My minister said, clearly, that this memorandum was not an agreement or even an agreement to agree; it was merely a memorandum of basic conditions and principles in the event that an agreement might eventually be concluded between Quebec and the federal government. This is, as was said by my hon. friend the minister of northern affairs, a set of guidelines and it is obvious that if one is to have guidelines one must express them in the indicative, not in the subjunctive mood; one must indicate them in the terms one would ordinarily find in the agreement itself. But, relying on sophistry, the hon. member for Yukon finds the word "agreement" in the memorandum and says: Aha! A fait accompli; a deal has been signed; the Eskimos have been betrayed. Yet the document is perfectly clear. We are still, as the minister was then, in the course of negotiations, and 1 would ask the hon. member for Yukon and other hon. members who, 1 know, are dealing sincerely with the subject, to consider these points as items in a memorandum made during the course of discussions.
1 listened while the minister referred to the declaration of a former minister of citizenship and immigration, Mrs. Fairclough, to be found recorded in the April 8, 1960, edition

of Hansard. The hon. lady announced government policy of that day to the effect that the federal government was then prepared to enact agreements with the governments of various provinces for the extension of normal provincial welfare services to persons residing on Indian reserves. She said the purpose was to allow the development of the Indians as a self-sufficient people so as to avoid the growth of exclusive welfare services on reserves-something which would tend to set Indians apart from other Canadians. This, as I understand it, is the point taken by the hon. member for Skeena.
The hon. member for Yukon answered this argument by saying that Eskimos are not Indians-that they are deliberately excluded from the Indian Act. This, I suggest to him, is another sophistry. The hon. member for Yukon looks at me benignly and smiles. He knows as well as I do that the governing authority is the supreme court action which he cited and which the hon. member for Peace River also cited-the Indian reference before the Supreme Court of Canada. I know that the hon. member for Yukon, a meticulous lawyer, still refers from time to time to the headnote, and the headnote summarizes the case: "Eskimo inhabitants of the province of Quebec are 'Indians' within the contemplation of head 24, section 91 of the British North America Act".

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: May I ask the hon. member a question? Is he referring to the 1939 supreme court decision?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: I anticipate a double-barreled reply.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Just one question, if that is the case referred to. Is the hon. member aware that the Indian Act was passed in 1951, which was 12 years after the decision to which he refers, with full knowledge that the decision he quoted says that a reference to an Indian does not include any person of the race of aborigines commonly referred to as Eskimos?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
I will concede, within the limits of the Indian Act and the welfare provisions of that section, the strength of the hon. member's argument. All I am saying is that we must not be legalistic about this. We are talking about the native people, and the principle adduced by the hon. member for Skeena, with which I agree. It is that the native, indigenous people must be allowed to develop and live as ordinary Canadian citizens, and be treated under the ordinary provincial jurisdictions of this country, whether they be Indians or Eskimos.
That is to say, they should eventually fall within the welfare provisions, the educational
Supply-Northern Affairs provisions and the provisions affecting natural resources which fall under provincial jurisdiction. I submit that the principle adduced by Mrs. Fairclough in her statement in 1960 is as valid in affecting the Eskimos as it is valid in affecting the Indians. For the hon. member for Yukon to try to introduce a legalistic distinction as affecting that principle surely is a late evening whimsy on his part.
The right hon. Leader of the Opposition said earlier today that we must not treat the Eskimos as voiceless serfs, as pawns, as political captives; and I could not agree more. As I understand it, the policy of the government with respect to the Indians and our native peoples is that they shall no longer remain as second class citizens; they shall no longer remain as wards of the federal government; they shall no longer remain as pawns, but shall be allowed to run the ordinary course of development as citizens, having the same rights and bearing the same responsibilities as any other Canadian. It is because that is envisaged within the negotiations undertaken by the federal government with the province of Quebec with respect to the Eskimos that the purpose of these negotiations, if they are ever to mature, surely is to emancipate the Eskimos as we hope one day to emancipate the Indians from federal trusteeship and allow them to develop as ordinary citizens in this country.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Only if they agree.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
The hon. member raises, probably by way of mental telepathy that is a product of a sensitive spirit, the next point I was going to make. This is our concern. We want the Eskimos to be brought into the 20th century; we want to encourage them to develop themselves as fully-fledged citizens of Canada, which means that eventually they must take the responsibility not only as citizens of this country but of their respective provinces. But we want to insist, and we have insisted, on certain guarantees before any transfer is effected. Those guarantees, which we are in the midst of negotiating, I would submit to the committee were set forth in the memorandum to which I referred earlier, namely the memorandum that my minister gave to this house on March 4; that the cultural and economic ties of the Eskimos throughout the north would not be broken; that the Quebec government would respect the Eskimo language and the religion to which they belong; that the Eskimos, after the transfer, would continue to enjoy at least the same services as they are now receiving. In other words, it was an integral part of any agreement to be negotiated with the province of

Supply-Northern Affairs Quebec that the same rights, the same services would be guaranteed to that northern, minority people.
The principle of self-determination has been raised and echoed in this chamber this evening. My minister made it quite clear that the governments of Canada and Quebec were to undertake to consult jointly with the Eskimos. What did this consultation mean? The statement has been read several times in this chamber. The hon. member for Yukon looks at me knowingly again. He knows exactly what those words mean. They are too clear to be mistaken except by a man who wants to mistake them.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: I am waiting for your interpretation.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Consultation in an impartial fashion means that a commission, which would be chosen jointly by both 'governments-

speechtext: Will there be Eskimos on it?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: He has done nothing of the kind.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, it is getting late in the evening and I know the hon. member for Yukon likes to maintain his seat and exercise his voice. But he must opt too; either speak, or sit. I do not say that unkindly.

speechtext: It might be the same thing.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Why don't you say something while you are on your feet?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, it is strange how good humour increases on the other side as the hour gets later.
The consultation would take the form of a commission chosen jointly by the two governments. Any agreement, before execution, would be submitted to the Eskimos, explained to them and interpreted to them. They would be asked for their views.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, would the hon. member permit a question?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Perhaps the hon. member would allow me to finish. Their views would be sought, and if as a result of those views, as a result of the expression of opinion from the Eskimos in the north, in Ungava and northern Quebec, the federal government deemed that modifications or changes to any draft agreement, if and when it is drafted, were necessary, those changes, to the best of my understanding, would be made. Let me say-

speechtext: Would the hon. member permit a question?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES

speechtext: Oh, oh.
