maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Order, please. The parliamentary secretary has the floor.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Would the hon. member permit a question?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: If the parliamentary secretary wished to accept a question, he would resume his seat. He has not done so, and therefore I presume he is not prepared to accept a question.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the hon. member for Yukon reminds me a great deal of Pandora and the genie which escaped from her box. Once you open the box, it is very difficult to put the genie back in. Let me say, in all fairness, that I believe those on the government side gave a fair hearing both to the hon. member for Yukon and the hon. member for Northwest Territories and I would appreciate receiving, for a few more minutes, the kind attention that I am wont to receive from the other side.
Those are the principles that this government, as I understand it, are trying to achieve; namely, emancipation of the native indigenous peoples of this country so that eventually they will be governed as ordinary Canadian citizens under provincial jurisdiction right across the country. The same principle, the same services and the same rights would be guaranteed to these minority, native peoples by whichever provincial government assumes responsibility for their administration-not jurisdiction. Third, the views of these people will be obtained in as democratic a fashion as is practically possible.
Let me say a final word, Mr. Chairman. Ever since the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources assumed this portfolio he has given every consideration to this important question. I had the opportunity of being on the trip across the north with him last summer when, as the hon. member for Northwest Territories said, we bumped into him. I might say that not only did we bump into the hon. member for Yukon, but we could not shake him.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: You are not shaking him now, either.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: When my minister was up there he said on several occasions, and expressed it from his heart-and the right hon. Leader of the Opposition gave him credit for that this afternoon-that we want government, not by laws but by men. That was a sincere statement.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: The other way around.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: A government of men, not laws.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: No, the other way around.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Order.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I find it a strange thing that a subject that seems to have attracted the sincere discussion, criticism and opposition of men opposite, who are entitled to take that position, should be treated by them, when the government maintains and defends its case, in a sense of joviality and ridicule. It should be one thing or the other; either the committee takes this question of a minority people seriously, or it does not.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Your speech has been filled with fun.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
If it does take it seriously, I would ask the concession of hon. members opposite to let me finish on this personal note. I have every confidence, as I am sure everyone in this house has, that the minister of northern affairs will see that justice is done to the Eskimos of northern Quebec, and that they are consulted within the full principle of democracy, and their views taken into account. I have no doubt of that, nor has any member on this side of the house; and if hon. members on the opposite side were to probe their consciences, neither have they.
In conclusion I should like to quote this evening's editorial in the Ottawa Journal, not necessarily a publication favourable to this government. The editorial is entitled "Nouveau Quebec" and I will read three paragraphs into the record, if I may:
Outsiders should be careful, however, to note that the federal government is not insisting on maintaining its custodianship of Eskimos in the province of Quebec. The federal government knows well that in the constitutional or legal or geographic sense Quebec has the right to seek to take over this responsibility which some years ago it voluntarily rejected.
The federal government properly asks, however, that the Eskimos suffer no infringement of their freedom of choice in religion, education and representation.
It is a matter of basic principle, greatly complicated by ice, isolation, tradition, prejudice, economics and politics-a matter demanding the greatest of care and understanding.
In resuming my seat let me say that my minister and those who are negotiating with him have tried to maintain that care and understanding, and I would ask hon. members on the other side of the house to credit us with that and to devote to the problem the same non-partisan type of care and understanding.
Supply-Northern Affairs

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: While the hon. member is still on his feet would he permit a question which I wanted to ask him during his remarks. Would he not agree with me that the democratic thing to do would be to have representation on the commission to be appointed either from the Eskimo council or by their selection of an independent counsel?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: There are several ways of going about this, and in the negotiations they are being considered. Whatever avenue is chosen in setting up this commission, I can assure the hon. member on behalf of the minister that the democratic principles to which he paid service tonight and to which we both adhere will be fulfilled.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Now will the hon. member answer the question I asked, if he cares to, namely whether he agrees that the Eskimo people should be represented on that commission.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: I realize the impatience of the hon. member for Yukon if he does not get an answer which is satisfactory to him. In general this question has already been answered. Every opportunity will be given to the Eskimos to present their views to the commissioners, whoever they may be. Whether or not an Eskimo will become a member of the commission I cannot say, as the hon. member knows full well.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: May I put a question to the parliamentary secretary. Is the effect of the intent of the memorandum which was put on Hansard on March 4 to consummate an agreement to transfer?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Is the hon, member asking me a question?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Yes.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: That memorandum, as I understand it, forms the guidelines-it does not provide the exact language but it does form the guidelines-of any eventual agreement which is made or concluded between the two governments. That is all I can say to him, whether or not it is satisfactory to him.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
If the hon. member would look at a few of the words contained in the memorandum for a moment I think he will agree that the government of Canada has committed itself to the principle of transferring jurisdiction first and foremost. Naturally I will have to extract sections from the text instead of reading the whole thing, but I do not think I am extracting them out of context. The first part concerns an agreement as to certain things. Then towards the end of the first paragraph, as reported at page 506 of Hansard, it says:

Supply-Northern Affairs
-Canada is prepared to have Quebec administer Eskimo affairs as part of Quebec's general administrative responsibilities in the province-
The memorandum says that it is an understanding reached at the February 29 meeting and that Canada is prepared to have Quebec administer these things. This is an intent which exhibits a desire on the part of Canada.
Then further on we come to point No. 3 of the matters which are understood, which refers to after the transfer has taken place, indicating that there will be a transfer. Then point No. 4 uses this expression-my grammar is not as good as that of the hon. gentleman who talked of indicatives, subjunctives and the like:
4. The governments of Canada and Quebec undertake to consult-
Then it explains the consultation and interprets it as-
-the communication of the terms of the agreement, excluding however the financial provisions thereof.. .will be made through a commission-
And so on.
Then further on in the same paragraph it says:
The functions of this commission will be to explain the conditions of the agreement-
So that both governments agree that such consultation is a prior condition of the execution of the agreement. There is nowhere a solitary word about the acceptance of that agreement. I submit that this, coupled with the reluctance, hesitancy and hiding of explanations given by the minister and his parliamentary secretary, indicates that there has been a sell-out of the rights and interests of these people.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I rise to answer what began as a question and ended as a declaration. I must repeat that those items in the memorandum which the hon. member has just recited have to be read in conjunction with the preamble at the beginning of the statement of the minister, when he said:
The memorandum is not an agreement, nor is it an agreement to agree. It does constitute a statement outlining a consensus with respect to certain basic principles and conditions which, in the event of an agreement, are common to the two governments.
It is surely a common experience in negotiating a treaty, whether it be between two countries or an agreement between two provinces or a contract between two people, that in the midst of the negotiations you set out the terms which will be agreed on one by one; and if you finally get to the end of the agreement then you have the terms. But if you are not able to reach agreement, and in this instance if the federal government is not able to reach a satisfactory result with


regard to minority rights, or the standard of services, or the method of consultation, or the financial provisions, then this whole series of items which the hon. member for Skeena read will be wiped out. These are statements of principle in general form which have been agreed on in the event that there is an eventual understanding between the two jurisdictions. If there is not, then it is all wiped out. That is the way I must explain the matter to the hon. member.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: I have a supplementary question. Is it not a fact that the statement of the minister which appeared at the front of Hansard is merely his interpretation of what the understanding is, and that there is also another party to the agreement, the government of Quebec, which has its interpretation too? I submit that all we can concern ourselves with is, what does the understanding mean, what does the memorandum say, not what the minister thinks it says.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: If I may reply at this time, I want to say that I regret very much that the hon. member for Skeena seems to be joining in the view taken by the hon. member for Yukon, namely that if you assert anything and it is not denied in the house it becomes a fact.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: On a question of privilege, the minister should know full well that I have my own opinions and I do not have to join this element over here.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: It is mutual.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: That statement seems to be agreeable to both sides of the house. I cannot help saying, however, that there is a likeness of attitude and I want to tell him that when he uses that kind of language he is not being fair to me and he is not being fair to himself.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: You are not being fair to the Eskimo people.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
There are three or four provisions included and I want to tell the hon. member that up to this time we have made practically no progress on them at all with the officials of the province of Quebec. I want to tell him that so far as the whole matter of financial arangements is concerned, we have not even had one single meeting on finance with any officials of the province of Quebec. So far we have not got to the point where we can agree that this memorandum and its provisions should be the basis for arrangements with the province of Quebec. Yet the hon. member gets up and asserts that in his judgment the Eskimos are already sold out. I want to assure him and the house, which is more important than he is, that

there are no arrangements at all, and in respect of the memorandum that we drew up we have made practically no progress at all.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I was delighted at the way the parliamentary secretary started his remarks, by talking about sophistry, because I was sure that before he would finish he would show that he is an expert in that regard. I was really deeply touched by his remarks with regard to getting information from the minister, with regard to questions being asked and the minister trying to supply information, because I am sure that the parliamentary secretary and the minister are aware that the main complaint we on this side of the house have been making, not only about his department but about all departments, is the lack of information; and the reason more progress has not been made on the estimates is that we have not got enough dentists on this side of the house. We cannot yank out the information.
To remind the minister of where he goes wrong, and as an example of his question answering, I would refer him to the 9th of March when I asked him if tenders had been called for 140 Eskimo houses to be delivered at Waterways. I got no answer that day. The next day the Speaker suggested that the question should go on the order paper. I explained the urgency and pointed out that the minister appeared to have the information ready and I thought there was a possibility that he was perhaps making a mistake. The minister then proceeded to answer and began with the words:
I am pleased to reply to the hon. member's argument.
He was pleased to reply to the argument. This is the usual thing. We call for information and we get an argument. To this day there is no answer to my question on record in the house. I will admit that a week or so later when the minister was passing my door he was courteous enough to tell me that the number was 104, not 140, but there is nothing on the record to show it, and until he answered a question asked by an N.D.P. member there was nothing to show they were going to be delivered at Waterways. The urgency is borne out because I have just found out that the minister has put out a tender for another 75 houses to be delivered at Waterways.
Considering that it is one month to the day since I asked my question, and considering the length of time we have been trying to get some straight answers out of the government, I think that the remarks of the parliamentary secretary in making a speech of that kind constitute nothing more than effrontery. Since 1 am dealing with the matter 20220-126
Supply-Northern Affairs of these houses, Mr. Chairman, I should like to make the further point that it is not just a matter of getting some information but rather of getting the right information. When the minister said he would answer my argument he did not give the information asked for. He proceeded to give me some freight rates, on which he based his contention that the government was proceeding the right way, but every item of information he supplied was inaccurate.
He gave a truck rate to Hay River of $2.85 per hundredweight. I got a telegram the next day from the main trucker there saying that the truck rate was $1.70. The minister gave rates by barge which did not apply to that class of goods. He gave rates by rail which were out of line. In other words, every figure supplied by the minister was inaccurate. Yet they ask us to take their word that they are trying to give us information. We were given all this gratuitously by way of argument advanced by the minister. What I wanted to know was whether the government was really buying them. I wanted some information so I would know whether they were going to proceed further, but all I got was an argument and incorrect information.
Not only is the information inaccurate but it is silly, because between shipping by way of Yellowknife or Hay River or Waterways the information he gave works out to a difference of $20 per ton, and if the minister knows anything at all about the Northwest Territories he should know that the rates each way are competitive, or else all the goods would go one way. With a difference of $20 per ton it would be silly of anyone to think that he could compete going a different way. Not only was the information gratuitous and inaccurate but it was stupid, and it simply shows that the minister is so careless he does not care what type of information he gives the house.
There is another point which I have mentioned before. The department says it has a rule that it favours neither Yellowknife Transportation nor Northern Transportation and I have thought over the years that the department has tried to carry out fairly a policy of giving freight 50-50 to these two companies. In this instance the houses are to be delivered at Waterways where only Northern Transportation can operate, so they are not trying to be fair at all.
If the minister was at all concerned about the accuracy of his information and what it does to the people in my area he would know that by quoting figures as erroneous as these, which make it seem advantageous to ship by way of rail to Waterways, he is doing the greatest possible damage to all the truckers operating out of Edmonton. The parliamentary

Business of the House
secretary to the minister has tried to persuade us that they have some regard for the rights of people, including the Eskimos. I suggest that if they have any regard for the rights of people they should at least check their information and make sure they are not harming the truckers of Edmonton in the way they have by trying to discourage any shipper in Canada from shipping by that route. May I call it ten o'clock, Mr. Chairman?
